#3503. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3502. 40 Years Later, Top Gun's Most Famous Line Is Still The Greatest '80s Movie Quote

What makes an '80s movie unique? The decade gave humanity lots of horrors that still plague us today, from rampant capitalism, corporations running wild, the rise of the religious far-right, and an obsession with consumerism that is still dominating our lives. But it was also a time of impeccable pop culture, whether it was video games, music, or movies.

Indeed, the 1980s were a wild ride for film fans, with the rise of blockbusters and high concept genre movies with big visual effects paving the way for the IP dominance of the box office. The best '80s movies show the versatility of the medium of cinema, creating strong iconography and delivering one-liners that are remembered decades later.

That's why it's hard to think of a movie that's as quintessentially '80s as Tony Scott's "Top Gun." This is a maximalist movie that exudes iconography, with every exterior day scene being set at sunset, a loud pock-rock soundtrack, plenty of leather jackets, a rousing love of Americana, and old-fashioned American patriotism wrapped in incredibly vague Cold War-inspired politics. This is also a movie so filled with unbridled homoeroticism that it became a gay classic, thanks to a warm story about male friendships that's also so steamy hot that sweaty muscled men are constantly talking about wanting each other's asses while standing half-naked.

Is "Top Gun" the best '80s movie? Probably not, but it is representative of the decade. This movie is an exercise in over indulgence, a movie that's endlessly entertaining and also dumb as hell. The overt military propaganda makes "Top Gun" essentially the movie version of the "Yvan eht nioj" music video from "The Simpsons."

Though the movie has plenty of great lines, one stands out as the most '80s movie quote.

The quote comes early in the movie, when Lt. Pete "Maverick" Mitchell (Tom Cruise) and his wingman LTJG nick "Goose" Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards) are walking down the tarmac on the way to their jets for a new assignment. When a fellow student tells Maverick that his rival Iceman (Val Kilmer) has won yet another contest, the cocky Maverick puts on a fake smile and just replies "I feel the need..." before Goose chimes in and the two say in unison, "The need... for speed!" before doing a high five.

It's a ridiculous moment, a cheesy line with an even cheesier delivery from Cruise and Edwards, but it captures the tone of "Top Gun" — loud, proud, and willing to have fun.

In the context of the movie, however, the line is also important to understanding Maverick. As his call sign implies, Maverick is reckless, and his impulsive behavior makes him a dangerous liability in the eyes of the academy and the military. Sure, Maverick brings results, but he is unreliable, especially compared to Iceman, who is just as good while also being able to follow commands.

"I feel the need, the need for speed" encapsulates not only Maverick's love for danger and for speed but also his insecurities and competitiveness. It's the ultimate expression of American individualism in "Top Gun," the belief of pushing yourself beyond your limits or not giving up when someone surpasses you. It's a declaration of purpose and bravado.

"You are still dangerous. But you can be my wingman any time." — Iceman

"Son, your ego is writing checks your body can't cash." — Stinger

"I don't like you because you're dangerous." — Iceman

"God, he loved flying with you Maverick. But he would've done it anyway... without you. He'd have hated it, but he would've done it." — Carole

"I want somebody's butt, I want it now, I've HAD IT!" — Air Boss Johnson

"You're not going to be happy unless you're going Mach 2 with your hair on fire." — Charlie

There's always news coming out of the superhero genre, and this week's was a doozy. The internet exploded when it was revealed that James Gunn was stepping down as co-CEO of DC Studios, just four years after crafting the new shared universe (which is streaming with an HBO Max subscription). We've seen how fans reacted to Gunn's departure, and now previous comments about the shared universe are coming out... and they didn't age well.

Gunn's plans for the DCU are seemingly cooked, and there are countless questions about how the burgeoning shared universe will continue. Will Gods and Monsters continue as planned, or could the DCU as we know it end? Only time will tell, but an interview from Parade's Instagram featuring Clayface star Tom Rhys Harries carries extra weight now. He spoke enthusiastically about Gunn's role as CEO, saying:

I think I was prior to Clayface, a big DC fan. And what Peter and James are doing with that universe, I’m excited to see expanding. And I’m really proud to be a part of that.

Ouch. I can't imagine the whiplash that Harries must be feeling, just weeks after Clayface hit theaters. The 36-year-old actor transformed into the Clayface we know and love in the movie's final moments, but now it's unclear if we'll ever get to see him again. Will he finally get to fight Batman in the DCU? It's unclear, but these comments show just how unexpected the regime change at DC was.

Indeed, actors like Skyler Gisondo have been breaking their silence about Gunn's departure, and it looks like no one knows what's going to come next. Gunn and Peter Safran originally listed a long list of projects that would be coming together, but who knows what their replacement Jeremy Latcham will do with the shared universe.

You can see Tom Rhys Harries's comments about the DCU below:

A post shared by PARADE Magazine (@parademag)

Fans are bummed that DC's shared universe has once again hit a huge setback, with moviegoers wondering if we'll ever get a bona fide shared universe like the MCU. The previous DCEU started strong with Zack Snyder's trilogy of movies, but it largely abandoned crossovers and interconnected stories in the years that followed. James Gunn was crafting his own cohesive universe, although now we're left with more questions than answers.

By all accounts, actors who worked with James Gunn and Peter Safran seem to have enjoyed their time collaborating with them in the DCU. But after Supergirl flopped at the box office and Clayface wasn't a home run, it sounds like the decision was made to find new leadership. Hopefully we get some information about what Latcham is planning.

The next upcoming DC movie hitting theaters is Man of Tomorrow on July 9, 2027. That movie is already shot and directed by Gunn himself, so smart money says the publicity tour is going to get awkward.

#3499. The Expanse: Osiris Reborn Shows Off Promising Gameplay in New Trailer

Visit an abandoned asteroid mine with the crew in The Expanse: Osiris Reborn latest trailer

The 44th annual Golden Joystick Awards opened the 2026 video game awards season. Beyond celebrating and rewarding the year's best games, the ceremony also featured exciting announcements and reveals. Owlcat Games shared an in-depth look at its upcoming sci-fi action RPG, The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, with the premiere of a new gameplay trailer. The 3-minute video unveiled interesting details about the 24th-century setting, gameplay mechanics, and exploration sites.

The Expanse is a novel series written under the pen name James S. A. Corey, used by co-authors Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck. It has been adapted for television into a critically-acclaimed series, and it will now return in the form of a video game called The Expanse: Osiris Reborn. Sci-fi enthusiasts are always on the lookout for a new space-faring game, so with a Spring 2027 release, this might just be players' next pick.

The "Becoming a Captain" trailer showcases a mission where the protagonist has to rescue a group of rebellious teens who have escaped to an abandoned asteroid mine riddled with space pirates. Players must speak to a specific NPC at a bar and accept his request to initiate this mission. It is entirely optional but extremely rewarding; completing the mission and bonding with one of the teens, Polly, might get her to join the player's crew later on. This will give players access to her special ability, which spawns a swarm of nanobots — a feature we see in the trailer.

Besides companion abilities, the players will have access to an array of other skills. In the trailer, we see them activate a spatial detection device, throw a small explosive projectile directly at the chest of a pirate, and launch a lethal device at an enemy behind cover. Gameplay isn't only about fun gadgets, though. The Expanse series is known for trying to avoid bending the rules of science. Osiris Reborn appears to be taking the same approach, as we can see from the lack of exterior sound during space fights on the asteroid. You can also notice the protagonist jump from one surface to another and easily stick to them in zero gravity, presumably wearing magnetic boots.

Fans of the franchise are happy to see the return of the series, even if it is through a completely different medium. However, Osiris Reborn isn't exclusive to fans of this universe; whether you're a sci-fi fan, a video game enthusiast looking for a fun RPG, or a heartbroken Mass Effect fan looking for your next story-driven space odyssey, this might just be the right game for you.

#3498. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3497. Victorian Psycho Review: Maika Monroe Goes Crazy In This Erratic Mix Of Humor And Horror

Horror-comedies tend to lean heavier on the "comedy" side of things than the "horror." But Zachary Wigon's "Victorian Psycho" attempts to do the opposite, giving the audience a gaggle of gruesome, unsettling moments punctuated by wry humor. It makes for an erratic viewing experience — you begin to feel the film would be better served staying in one lane rather than trying to make concepts like dead babies funny. Regardless, "Victorian Psycho" mostly succeeds due to Maika Monroe, who gives everything she's got as Winifred Notty, a psychotic governess who moves in with a wealthy family and proceeds to pile up a body count.

Her attempt at an English accent may be a bit spotty, but Monroe's commitment to playing crazy ultimately works, and works well. Her wry narration guides us through outlandish, blood-drenched moments as she spins a twisted tale. If the film's title (an obvious nod to "American Psycho") wasn't a dead giveaway, it's clear from the jump that Winifred is ... not well. A suspicious past follows her as she arrives at Ensor House, inhabited by the Pounds family.

Winifred may be deranged, but the Poundses aren't exactly a pleasant bunch. Mr. Pounds (Jason Isaacs) is oblivious, Mrs. Pounds (Ruth Wilson) is cruel and ruthless with the staff, and the children Andrew (Jacobi Jupe) and Drusilla (Evie Templeton) have their own issues (Andrew is a brat destined to grow up to be a bully and Drusilla is more than a little creepy). A sane person would take one look at the Pounds family and head for the hills, but of course, Winifred isn't sane.

There's plenty of room for fun here, but "Victorian Psycho" is never confident enough in what it's trying to do. The performances are all very broad and big, save for the always-welcomed Thomasin McKenzie, playing the good-natured but clueless nurse Ms. Lamb, who becomes Winifred's only real friend (and instantly buys into her quickly concocted story about a ghoul roaming the grounds of Ensor House).

As big and over-the-top as many of the elements here are, "Victorian Psycho" also seems to be trying to make a point about the subjugation of women in polite society. Yet it has no real insight into this beyond a surface level approach, and it's hard to get caught up in any sort of message when the film is also constantly pointing out how ridiculous everything here is.

Wigon, who previously directed "Sanctuary," piles on some energetic camerawork that frequently mirrors Winifred's fractured mind, but the script by Virginia Feito, adapting her own novel, relies too much on incessant narration that's not nearly as funny as it should be. And yet, "Victorian Psycho" remains perpetually watchable primarily due to Monroe's performance. A certified scream queen at this point in her career, it's a lot of fun to see Monroe cut loose and swing an axe at people's heads.

"Victorian Psycho" is just a little too unstable for its own good. There's a specific reason why Winifred has shown up at Ensor House, but the slow reveal of what's going on here feels undercooked. And when the film reaches its grand guignol finale, Wigon inexplicably starts pulling punches, robbing "Victorian Psycho" of a more satisfying conclusion and instead attempting something far more serious and dramatic than everything we've seen so far.

What this all comes down to is me wanting to like "Victorian Psycho" a lot more than I ultimately did. I enjoyed Monroe's performance, and the film's morbidly funny atmosphere, but I came away from it all a tad unsatisfied. There's a ghoulish charm to the narrative, but the blood and guts of something far better is lurking somewhere in here, just out of sight.

"Victorian Psycho" opens in theaters on November 13, 2026.

#3496. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3495. Ocarina of Time Fans Should Check Out This Zelda-Inspired TTRPG That Just Hit Stores

After a successful BackerKit campaign, Twilight Sword is now available on retail

The Legend of Zelda fans are eating well right now. The franchise is celebrating its 40th anniversary with the remake of Ocarina of Time, which was released on Nov. 5 to rave reviews and became the second best-selling game on the Nintendo Switch 2 in less than a week. Sony Pictures is releasing a live-action film adaptation in April 2027. Now you can share the feel of exploring Hyrule with friends with the tabletop role-playing game Twilight Sword, which launched in gaming stores this week and has already smashed through the goal for its next crowdfunding campaign.

Italian studio Two Little Mice raised €701,000 ($77,700) for Twilight Sword on BackerKit in 2026, crushing its €10,000 ($12,000) goal in just 24 hours. The game’s co-creators told Polygon they wanted to capture the feeling of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom at the gaming table, evoking Link’s journey with a modular map revealed by flipping cards representing new regions. The game also has a rich cooking and brewing system, and fast and intuitive combat.

Players take on the role of Champions who have been awakened by the Spirits to protect the land of Radia from the dark knight Vardas and his army of monsters. An original d12-based Created by Twilight rules system revolves around gathering Hope by exploring, helping NPCs, and defeating bosses. Hope is used to counter Despair, the corruption that blocks off areas of the map until players are strong enough to advance.

The $51 Twilight Sword Core Rulebook includes everything you need to create characters, including feats, classes, and equipment. It also provides an overview of the world and some monsters and bosses you might encounter. The $45 Lands of Radia book adds extra character options and everything you need to run a campaign, including travel event tables, landmarks, quest hooks, and key NPCs. The $42 Card Chest includes map pieces to reveal during exploration and cards representing monsters, weapons, feats, and spells to make it easy to keep track of everything. All purchases made through Free League Publishing include a PDF via DrivethruRPG.

Two Little Mice seized on the momentum by launching another BackerKit campaign on the same day as Twilight Sword’s retail release. The Twilight Sword & Monster Book has already raised €371,000 ($411250). Expected to release in October 2027, the book will add more character options and monsters, plus tools for the game master to create their own enemies. It also expands on the crafting system by providing rules to collect monster parts to turn into gear. Add-ons include a GM screen, a Battle Chest with standees representing monsters from all the Twilight Sword books, and a Monster Chest filled with new monster and monster gear cards. The campaign runs through Dec. 3.

#3494. Who Plays Thrain In The Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power Season 3

You shall not pass! This article contains minor spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episodes 1-4.

After two years, "The Rings of Power" is back and as sprawling as ever. In fact, it may be even more so than it already was. Seasons 1 and 2 of the Prime Video series took us all over the map (quite literally, thanks to all those nifty map transitions), from the island kingdom of Númenor far in the West to the volcanic wastes of Mordor in the East. Season 3 expands the borders of Middle-earth even further, taking us to new locations and introducing multiple new characters to keep track of — some of whom seem more trustworthy than others.

Somewhere in the middle of all this is the Dwarf prince known as Thráin, the elder brother of King Durin (Owain Arthur) and a figure referenced with no small amount of suspicion towards the end of Season 2. As viewers quickly find out upon returning to Khazad-dûm, there is a fair bit of internal strife going on within the underground city, and Thráin's arrival only exacerbates the tension in the air. While this is actually an original character created solely for the show, he still requires quite a lot of nuance and complexity to fully bring him to life.

So, who better to do so than character actor Eddie Marsan? Yes, it might be incredibly difficult to tell who's actually playing the stoutly Dwarf underneath that mountain of prosthetics, makeup, and that bushy mane of flaming red hair. But, if you take notice of those piercing eyes and distinctive voice, you just might be able to recognize the talents of a performer you've definitely seen before.

As it turns out, maybe there are some Dwarves that you can only trust as far as you can toss them (with respect to Gimli). While watching Thrain do his mischievous thing throughout the early episodes of "The Rings of Power" this season, you'll likely find yourself wondering what else you've seen Eddie Marsan appear in before. In a quirk of scheduling, his most recent high-profile role was actually in this year's "Clayface," where he portrayed Frank Fitzpatrick. As the shady talent manager to Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), this is a perfect example of the kind of slippery character Marsan plays so well. Before that, he popped up in three episodes of the Netflix series "Heartstopper" and had supporting roles in three of director Guy Ritchie's most recent movies: "Operation Fortune: Ruse de Guerre," "Wrath of Man," and "The Gentlemen."

You'd have to go back a little further to pinpoint what might be his most well-known role of all, however. He was cast in the 2009 "Sherlock Holmes" film as the famous Inspector Lestrade, a role he would then reprise in the 2011 sequel "A Game of Shadows" (yes, both of which were also directed by Ritchie). Having worked regularly since the 1990s, the English actor can be seen in a prolific amount of titles over the decades. Some notable examples include Martin Scorsese's "Gangs of New York," the Wachowski Sisters' "V for Vendetta," "Mission: Impossible III," "Miami Vice," "The World's End," "Deadpool 2," and far too many more to name.

In short, Marsan is an acting veteran who knew exactly how to breathe life into a newly-arriving figure like Thráin.

New episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 premiere on Prime Video every Wednesday.

#3493. Stacy Keach, ‘Fat City’ and ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Dead at 85

Stacy Keach, the highly prolific screen and stage actor known to audiences for his television role as the private detective Mike Hammer and other tough guy characters, died of heart failure on Tuesday at his family residence in Magdalenka, Poland. He was 85.

Keach’s death was confirmed by his wife, Malgosia, in a statement sent by representation at Guttman Associates.

“It is with profound sadness and a broken heart that I announce the passing of my darling husband, Stacy Keach, who passed away on November 10, 2026, at our family home in Magdalenka, Poland,” reads the release. “After a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure, Stacy peacefully departed this world. He fought for so long, with extraordinary courage, determination and strength. He was a true warrior, facing his illness with the same remarkable spirit and resilience that defined his life.” Related Stories How Nicholas Britell Packs Conflicting Emotions Into the ‘Jay Kelly’ Score Adam Sandler Looks Back on His Early Days in Hollywood at IndieWire Honors

She continues: “Stacy was not only a legendary actor, admired and loved by audiences the world over, but also my beloved husband, my companion and the heart of our family. His passing leaves an immeasurable emptiness in our lives. But his extraordinary spirit, his unforgettable voice and the love he gave so generously will remain with us forever.”

Keach rose to the stature of one of the preeminent classical stage actors in the United States through the ’60s and 70s, venturing into avant garde productions and playing roles like Falstaff and Hamlet in his early career. He first appeared on Broadway in 1969, playing Buffalo Bill in Arthur Kopit’s “Indians,” for which he received a Tony nomination. He was also a four-time Drama Desk award winner.

It was after establishing his onstage bona fides that Keach was tapped to play the detective Mike Hammer for CBS’ television film “Murder Me, Murder You,” adapting the character of Mickey Spillane novels that had previously been brought to the screen in noirs like “Kiss Me Deadly.” The film spawned a three-season run of “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer,” with nearly 50 episodes and two more TV movies featuring Keach as the tough PI. A revival, “Mike Hammer, Private Eye,” was produced in the late ’90s.

In film, Keach established his star in 1972 with early featured roles in John Huston’s classic boxing drama “Fat City” and Richard Fleischer’s intense cop thriller “The New Centurions,” along with a starring role of Doc Holliday in Frank Perry’s 1971 Western “Doc.” Though he never quite rose to marquee stardom, Keach’s character actor skills were called upon regularly by Hollywood, oftentimes playing military authorities in titles ranging from “Up in Smoke” to “Escape from L.A.” to “Truth.” In 1980, he starred in, co-wrote and executive produced the Walter Hill Western “The Long Riders,” alongside his brother James Keach.

Other notable credits for Keach include the lead of “Exorcist” creator William Peter Blatty’s horror oddity “The Ninth Configuration” (1980), the voice of the mysterious villain Phantasm in the classic superhero animated feature “Batman: Mask of the Phantasm” (1993), and the Bakersfield-loving father to George Clooney’s movie star in “Jay Kelly” (2025).

Born June 2, 1941 in Savannah, Ga., Walter Stacy Keach Jr.’s family moved to Pasadena after his drama teacher father signed a day-player contract with Universal. Keach attended University of Calfornia, Berkeley and later studied theater at Yale School of Drama and the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art.

Along with Malogisa, Keach is also survived by his their children, Karolina and Shannon; their grandchildren; their spouses; and his brother, James.

#3492. This Low-Profile Roborock Vacuum and Mop Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but prices aren’t always what they seem. Use a price tracker to make sure you’re getting the best deal, or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3491. ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

The major Hollywood studios tend to shy away from the subject of class warfare because they know they can’t pull them off with a straight face. But young people in this country are increasingly animated by radical leftist ideas like “earning a livable wage” and “being able to buy a home before they die,” and at a certain point the movies will have to meet them where they live. Perhaps that point is now. How else to explain why Jeff Bezos would fund a Robin Hood-esque heist thriller that not only encourages its target demographic to commit armed robberies, but also kinda sorta teaches them how? (No one is going to confuse a David Leitch movie for “The Anarchist Cookbook.”) At a time when internet activists like Hasan Piker have come to occupy more space in the public imagination than Marvel superheroes, selling the masses on fanciful stories about the downward redistribution of wealth might be the billionaire class’ best protection against the threat of it actually happening in real life. It’s a lot more fun than paying a proportional tax rate, at least. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

Of course, the poppy and frenetic “How to Rob a Bank” wouldn’t dare to take aim at massive corporations that widen the wealth gap by destroying small businesses, normalizing exploitative labor practices, and accelerating worldwide environmental collapse. This is very specifically a film about how banks are bad and should be fucked with, an opinion that the founder of Amazon might actually share with the average ticket-buyer.

And it’s not like the director of “Bullet Train” suddenly made a serious call to action that’s poised to inspire a wave of copycat robberies. Shot with all the propulsiveness of “Trainspotting” but almost none of its unbridled lust for life, Leitch’s YouTube-era fairy tale is no more dangerous to America’s power structures than “Verity” or “Project Hail Mary” (to name some of its studio’s other recent titles). Compared to the lawlessness of “Grand Theft Auto VI,” it might as well be the “Ocarina of Time” remake “Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.” Still, its cast is hot, its heart is in the right place, and while the Amazon Punk of it all has a tendency to make its fantasy seem more like a sale, there’s something indivisibly real and relatable to the premise of a heist movie whose characters feel like they have to steal the most basic principles of the life they were promised.

Ryan (Nicolas Hoult, channeling a very effective smidgeon of the destructive intensity that made him so terrifying in “The Order”) isn’t trying to get rich or spark a revolution, he and his accomplices just want a fair shot at the same thing that previous generations have been afforded as part of the American contract: The chance to support his family, and maybe a fair shot at revenge against the people and/or system who denied him that opportunity. In most respects, that shot has never been more unfair than it is now, but the internet — which has become the most powerful system for socioeconomic oppression this side of sharecropping — has turned attention into a currency more valuable than cash, and young people are still inventing new ways to harness those riches for themselves.

For Ryan, that process starts with stealing money the old-fashioned way, as he and his four-person crew film themselves knocking off every bank in Pittsburgh (their identities protected by giant animal masks). But the cash seems to be less important than the content that it buys them, as the gang’s real passion is reserved for the splashy, hi-octane YouTube tutorials that Hugo (an upbeat Rhenzy Feliz) cuts together and posts online after each job. “You know what’s more powerful than a gun?,” Ryan says. “An audience.” That’s us! We rule.

What the animal brigade plans to use that audience for is a mystery for most of the movie, but the big reveal is satisfying enough so long as you’re willing to accept your hard-edged socioeconomic commentary with a side of “The Thomas Crown Affair”-flavored silliness. Slapped with titles like “Lowkey Best Heist Ever,” the videos proselytize against complacency, as Ryan — still disguised as “The Wolf,” despite the fact that Hoult’s blond dye job makes his blue eyes pop like crazy — informs the masses that the odds of earning six figures in this economy are less than half the odds of pulling off an armed robbery. Sure, pulling something off isn’t the same thing as getting away with it, but who has time to quibble when they’re being fucked to death by the one percent?

And every member of Ryan’s crew has been done rather dirty. Iraq War vet Vince (an affectingly subdued Pete Davidson as the resident gun expert) has learned the hard way that “a country you fight for may not fight for you,” while Ryan shares a tragic backstory with his partner and getaway driver Emi (a wildly underused Anna Sawai) that only comes out after Mark Bianculli’s script pulls the ripcord on its propulsive first half and settles into its characters’ flimsiness during the comparatively leaden stretch that follows. We never learn anything about how the crew found each other, and unlike in the “Fast & Furious” saga, that familial energy fails to galvanize into something bigger than the sum of its parts.

Still, Hoult could get the job done by channeling even a smidgeon of the destructive intensity that he brought to “The Order,” and the religious fervor he instills in Ryan’s mission is enough to keep “How to Rob a Bank” moving forward even when the film is just spinning its wheels. Or, as the case might be, when the film pivots to a parallel track that never meaningfully overlaps with the main plot.

It’s hard to be mad at this movie for casting John C. Reilly as the Al Pacino in an eat the rich Gen-Z “Heat” (not when he gets to bark things like “Put some fucking pepper on it!” at his subordinates), or for pairing him with Zoë Kravitz as a grungy hacker who’s roped into the case in exchange for her freedom (and use of her glossed-over surveillance software), but the mild comedy of their mismatched vibe never compensates for how disconnected they both are from the main plot. Whatever inter-generational friction is gained — and then smoothed over — between them in a movie that makes bizarrely little attempt to weave them into Ryan’s tale. For all of its hashtag agitprop, “How to Rob a Bank” isn’t nearly high-minded enough to justify putting ideas before its plot, and it’s an enormous self-own that Kravitz never so much as interacts with the Hoult side of things.

Be that as it may, Leitch leans into the movie’s digital revolution as hard as circumstances allow, and what his film sometimes lacks in detail or precision it strives to compensate for with smiling verve and some bone-crunching action (there isn’t enough physical violence for this to stack up to the rest of 87North Productions’ body of work, but it’s nice that Leitch shoehorns a few solid brawls into the mix just because he can). Not since “The Perks of Being a Wallflower” has a studio movie gotten so much out of Pittsburgh, and the overbroad political messaging of “How to Rob a Bank” is sharpened by its rich sense of place, and specifically the way its locations reflect the story’s larger collision between the old world and the new.

That temporal confusion is well-served by a film that resolves as more of a fairy tale than anything else — a heist movie full of talking animals, and one that hinges on YouTube as a modern form of spellcasting. It’s all just real enough to suggest that we have the power to make it realer.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “How to Rob a Bank” in theaters on Friday, November 13.

#3490. 5 Years Ago Today: Andrew Garfield Gave An Oscar-Worthy Performance In A Netflix Movie

There are, in my estimation, many actors who should have Oscars who don't. Amanda Seyfried should have one (and might be eligible for one in 2027 thanks to one of 2026's most confounding films). Amy Adams' various near-misses have led her to stumble headfirst into awful Oscar bait projects like "Hillbilly Elegy." John Goodman has never even been nominated. When it comes to the best actors who don't have Academy Awards, the list is long ... and Andrew Garfield is definitely on it.

Garfield, who rose to prominence in projects like "Doctor Who" and "Lions for Lambs" before earning international fame and acclaim for his pivotal role in "The Social Network," is genuinely one of the most talented performers of his generation. You could point to any number of his projects and make a case, but I'm going to say that Garfield should have an Oscar for playing "Rent" writer Jonathan Larson in the 2021 movie musical "Tick... Tick... Boom!" (for which he did earn a Best Actor nomination).

Even if you're not a reformed musical theater kid like me, you know about "Rent" — but generally, we need to talk about "Tick... Tick... Boom!" way more. Before "Rent," Larson — who died at the age of 35 in 1996 after suffering from an aortic dissection — penned the mostly-autobiographical "Tick... Tick... Boom!" about his struggles to make it in musical theater, coming on the heels of his failed futuristic musical "Superbia." Initially written as a solo show performed just by Larson on piano, the musical got a full-length treatment thanks to David Auburn after Larson's tragic passing, and "Hamilton" and "In the Heights" scribe Lin-Manuel Miranda adapted it into a film that released on November 12, 2021. Garfield's performance as Larson is electrifying, pitch-perfect, and gripping, and he should have an Oscar for it.

The "plot" of "Tick... Tick... Boom!" is relatively simple — Andrew Garfield plays Jonathan Larson as he works days at the Moondance Diner and spends his free time perfecting that aforementioned musical "Superbia" for an upcoming workshop. Along the way, he grapples with the idea of leaving the arts behind for a more lucrative and stable career — like his best friend Michael (Robin de Jesús), who works for an ad agency — while also stressing about turning 30 years old.

If you're familiar with "Rent," you may not be surprised to learn that the HIV-AIDS crisis plays a role; his friend Freddy (Ben Levi Ross) is HIV-positive, and it's eventually revealed that Michael is as well. As Jonathan tries to manage his personal and professional lives, he crosses paths with his idol Stephen Sondheim (played by Bradley Whitford, though the real Sondheim did lend his voice to an answering machine message before he passed away in 2021) and frets about whether or not "Superbia" has any chance of success.

Usually, the gift of hindsight doesn't really serve an actor, but I think knowing that Larson passed away before "Rent" won a Pulitzer Prize (and Tonys) gives Garfield a great perspective here. His Jonathan is frenetic, a live wire, and lives his life to the fullest; Garfield's passionate performance throughout the film paints a picture of a man who's running out of time, and even though that's obviously expressed through the character's anxieties about turning 30, it's also a poignant representation of an artist whose life was cut tragically short ... and in numbers like "Why," "30/90," and "Louder than Words," Garfield pays perfect homage to Larson's life and legacy.

I think I've been pretty clear about the fact that Andrew Garfield should have an Oscar for "Tick... Tick... Boom!" He should, however, have won his second Oscar for that movie — because Garfield should have an Academy Award for best supporting actor for playing Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in "The Social Network."

Under careful direction from David Fincher and working with one of Aaron Sorkin's all-time best scripts — which he ultimately betrayed with his dog-brained sequel "The Social Reckoning" — Garfield is extraordinary as Eduardo, best friend to Jesse Eisenberg's Mark Zuckerberg who provides money and support during the initial founding of Facebook. In one timeline, we see Mark and Eduardo as Harvard University students trying to get their social media platform off the ground; in another, we see Eduardo suing Mark after Mark cruelly cuts Eduardo out of the company and brings his shares down drastically on the advice of new partner Sean Parker (a ridiculously well-cast Justin Timberlake).

Garfield should probably have several awards just for the way he delivers the line "Sorry, my Prada's at the cleaners, along with my hoodie and my f***-you flip flops" to Eisenberg's Mark after he discovers his betrayal ... but throughout the entire film, he's uniformly excellent as a man whose closest friend is also the most destructive force in his life. Garfield needs to be taken more seriously as an actor across the board, and an Oscar nomination for "Tick... Tick... Boom!" is a good start. In my opinion, though? He should be swimming in a pool full of trophies every day when he wakes up ... and he should have Oscars for "The Social Network" and "Tick... Tick... Boom!" Because the musical is a Netflix original, you can screen it there and see for yourself.

#3489. Sega Almost Had a Legit Madden Competitor — Until EA 'Sabotaged' It

A bit of games industry subterfuge you didn’t see in the Madden movie

Trip Hawkins isn’t the sort of guy who’s afraid to take a risk and bet big. He founded Electronic Arts in 1982, around the same time that Atari’s fortunes were fading — and threatening to take the entire video games industry down with it. Ever since he was a kid, he’d wanted to create his own football simulation game, first as a tabletop experience, and later as a computer game for the Apple II and Commodore 64.

Hawkins is a major character in David O. Russell’s new film Madden, which hits theaters this week. It traces the football icon’s journey from coach to commentator to video game legend. Early in the story, Hawkins (John Mulaney) approaches Madden (Nicolas Cage) at a glitzy afterparty for Super Bowl XI in 1977, moments after the Oakland Raiders clinched their first NFL championship. Hawkins eagerly pitches a football computer game, but the coach is understandably distracted by the thrill of the occasion.

Hawkins keeps trying as the years tick by, eventually getting Madden’s ear during a cross-country bus trip. (Madden was notoriously afraid of flying and was driven to NFL games each week in a custom Greyhound bus called the Madden Cruiser.) Though the film takes some creative license with the timeline of how the game series came to life, Hawkins told Polygon in an interview ahead of Madden’s release that it gets a lot right about his relationship with the football icon.

“I was plotting and maneuvering for over a decade before I founded Electronic Arts. I was planning and preparing over a long period of time,” Hawkins said. “But I certainly didn't have the budget to go to Miami and try to sneak into a Super Bowl party.”

Overall, Hawkins sees the film as an accurate portrayal of both sides of the John Madden he knew: a calculating on-field strategist and a Turducken-loving primetime commentator.

“When you're dealing with John in a business setting, he's deadly serious. And while he's deadly serious and also dropping an F-bomb like every third word, John is a very intelligent guy. This is just one example of how smart he is — he never had a problem needing to get bleeped, you know, when he was on the air,” Hawkins explained.

“He figured out how to communicate with everybody,” Hawkins added. “He created a persona that was kind of emphasizing the lovable side of him, the big bear side of him. It was pretty clever of him to just create a character that he got to play as an announcer.”

The massive popularity of the Madden games is a major plot point in the film, but the series’ outsized role in the console wars of the early 1990s is only referenced obliquely. Armed with Madden’s original playbooks from the Oakland Raiders — yes, that plot point really did happen IRL — Hawkins was ready to bring John Madden Football to a 16-bit console. But he didn’t want to deal with Nintendo’s pricey third-party licensing. Instead, a team within EA spent a year reverse-engineering the Sega Genesis. That meant EA could produce software without Sega's assistance, which gave them leverage to negotiate more favorable licensing terms with Nintendo’s biggest rival.

“I basically called Sega and said, ‘Look, this is what we've done. You know, we can all go to court and have a big lawsuit and waste everybody's time. Or we can be partners and work together in the marketplace and try to beat out Nintendo in this 16-bit market segment.’ We were able to work out a lucrative arrangement where we could do that. And they knew that if they didn't make it a really good deal for me, I would just go do it on my own anyway,” Hawkins explained.

Sega was working on a football game of its own, Joe Montana Football. Like Madden, it was set to be released in time for the holiday season of 1990, shortly after the Genesis launched in North America. But development wasn’t going according to plan. Sega CEO Hayao Nakayama called Hawkins in a panic, asking if he’d be willing to “cancel” Madden and instead release the game under the name Joe Montana Football. Hawkins came up with a clever solution that worked for both EA and Sega.

“Of course, I'm thinking to myself, ‘I really don't wanna disappoint him and our relationship is really important to me, but there's no way I'm gonna do that,’” Hawkins said. “I knew that this debut 16-bit game was a really great NFL football game. I knew it was gonna be the pivot point for EA Sports, and it was gonna really be able to make it take off. And as it turned out, I was able to tell Sega, ‘We're still gonna put Madden Football out. ‘But I'll make Montana Football for you also.’ And of course, like 98% under the hood is the program code from Madden Football. And I just gave a facelift and, no offense intended, but I sabotaged the game to make it inferior to our game.”

“The Montana game that we made had maybe less than 10% of the number of plays that we had at the Madden game,” Hawkins added. “I was able to deliver them the final version of Montana in six weeks.”

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Joe Montana Football omitted Madden’s pseudo-3D field and reduced the playbook from 113 plays to 13. Even so, Montana sold more than two million copies, compared to Madden’s 400,000. Still, Madden was a massive hit for EA and spawned a sequel the following year. The series has gone on to sell more than 150 million copies. For Hawkins, the last-minute project was worth it to get the game he’d been dreaming about for so long in players’ hands.

“I thought to myself, ‘Well, their marketing budget is way bigger than mine.’ Sega's marketing is gonna dwarf what Electronic Arts can afford, and I don't want anybody to know that they're really, fundamentally the same game. I mean, our game's better, you know, we took a bunch of stuff out,” Hawkins explained. “But that was part of the contract, that they couldn't tell anybody where the game came from.”

Madden may not have touched on a lot of the behind-the-scenes games industry lore, but Hawkins says the coach was just as fond of talking about his namesake video game over a heaping plate of Santa Maria barbeque as he is in the movie.

“Uh, yeah. We ate a lot of meat,” Hawkins recalled with a chuckle. “John is a big, big time eater.”

#3488. Netflix's Acclaimed Spy Series Now Streaming Season 2 Turns Q Into James Bond

The long-anticipated second season of Netflix’s spy thriller series Black Doves has arrived to fill the void left by Slow Horses. Black Doves feels like the Winter Olympics version of Slow Horses: it has the same blend of high-octane action spectacle and witty British banter, but with a classically Shane Black Christmas setting. Like Slow Horses, Black Doves subverts the usual James Bond formula with a gritty sense of realism and a dry sense of humor.

Keira Knightley is technically the lead of the series as Helen Webb, née Dawson, a secret agent who marries a politician she honeytrapped and gets drawn into a sinister conspiracy when her extramarital lover is killed. Knightley gives a terrific performance, and Helen is a compelling antihero in her own right, but her co-star Ben Whishaw steals the show. Helen is interesting enough to follow her story, but her colleague Sam Young is outright fascinating.

Sam is a friend of Helen’s who used to be a hitman and now springs into action whenever his old pal calls. Whishaw was the perfect meta casting for this role because, apart from Paddington Bear, his most iconic role is James Bond’s tech guy, Q, from the Daniel Craig era, and now, he’s essentially playing Bond himself. Much like Bond, Sam is a cold-blooded assassin with a license to kill. He’s as charming in bed as he is ruthless in the field, and he maintains a sardonic smirk through all his violent actions.

Just as Slow Horses has given us a chance to see Gary Oldman as an aging 007 archetype who’s still got it, Black Doves has given us a chance to see what Whishaw’s Bond would look like. Sam is both believably badass and surprisingly vulnerable, and Whishaw has made the most of that promotion out of the Q Branch.

The casting search is currently underway for the next actor to play Bond. Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson, and Nicholas Hoult are all reportedly under consideration to play 007 in Amazon’s upcoming reboot directed by Denis Villeneuve, and there’s at least one unannounced mystery actor who could still land the job.

There’s been a lot of discussion about whether to diversify the casting of 007, and whether Bond could be a woman or a person of color or a member of the LGBTQ+ community. The producers are unlikely to cast anyone other than a straight white man to play Bond — those five announced candidates all fit the traditional bill — so it’s up to other Bond-inspired media to imagine the other versions of the character we could have. Idris Elba’s turn as Luther is pretty close to what his 007 would look like, and Knightley’s portrayal of Helen in Black Doves is essentially a female Bond.

Black Doves has not only given us a female Bond; Whishaw’s Sam is the closest we’ve seen to a gay Bond. Sam has all the hallmarks of Bond: he’s a suave, charismatic killer-for-hire who rarely loses his cool, never misses a shot, and likes to sleep around. The only difference is that, instead of sleeping with women, he sleeps with men.

It’s refreshing to see a gay character whose main internal conflict has nothing to do with being gay. Throughout Black Doves, Sam is tormented by his grisly work and his flimsy code of ethics and the targets he’s forced to eliminate and the fact that he can never settle down with someone he loves and enjoy a nice, peaceful, normal life, but he’s completely at peace with being gay. That’s not what defines him; that’s just part of who he is, and that’s what good representation looks like.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. The rest of the U6 Pro lineup is discounted as well, so you can pick up the same TV in sizes from 55 inches to a massive 100 inches, for anyone with the room for something closer to a home-theater-sized screen. Whichever size you choose, you’ll get free delivery to the room of choice—a service that normally costs $19.99. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. Viewing angles are limited too, with the picture losing quality fairly quickly when you move off-center—and its built-in speakers aren’t particularly impressive either, so a soundbar could be worth budgeting for.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but prices aren’t always what they seem. Use a price tracker to make sure you’re getting the best deal, or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.
