#3486. Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers

Film lovers can make and post their fan edits legally thanks to Moonbeem, a distribution network for independent film. Fan edits are among the most-watched film content on social media, and nearly all of them are made from footage whose rights nobody cleared. But on Moonbeem, the rights holder decides which scenes to open and creators cut from those scenes. Moreover, every fan edit points viewers back to where the film can be rented, bought, or watched. Fan edits made this way have been viewed more than 190 million times across the network.

The company has unveiled its free panel for Adobe Premiere Pro, which is where the approved scenes will be available. The announcement comes during Adobe MAX, the tech company’s annual conference in Miami Beach, Florida. The company believes it’s one of the first times fans can cut real scenes from released films, with the rights holders’ permission, in the editing software they already use. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

With the panel, an editor picks a scene the filmmaker has cleared to use, pulls it onto the timeline, cuts, exports, and posts. The edit links back to the film, and approved edits can earn on funded campaigns. The panel is built on UXP and is live on Adobe Exchange.

Campaigns include “Erupcja,” released by 1-2 Special, whose fan edits have passed 4.6 million views,and “Bob Trevino Likes It,” from Roadside Attractions, at 5.6 million. Distributors on Moonbeem alsoinclude Magnolia Pictures, Oscilloscope Laboratories, and Antenna Releasing. The network isexpanding its list of partners globally.

“Every fan edit on Moonbeem exists because the film’s owner wanted it to,” said Dan Sickles, co-founder and CEO of Moonbeem and the director of the films “Dina” and “Mala Mala.” “Editors get real scenes inside the tool they already use, filmmakers get an audience sharing their stories, and we get to see what they make.”

The panel arrives as independent filmmakers look for a new home to host their work. Vimeo On Demand has been slowly phased out and will close on November 20. Moonbeem says it offers a “free migration bridge” that moves a seller’s films, prices and artwork without requiring a new upload. Past buyers will keep the films they paid for. Moonbeem said dozens of storefronts carrying over 350 films have moved so far.Moonbeem was incubated through the Sundance Institute’s Catalyst program and is based in Brooklyn.

#3485. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3484. Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer

Can a conservative “canceled” theater director rise from the ashes of his own ruination — and in this climate? That’s one of the questions top of mind for filmmakers Nicholas Clark and Dylan Frederick, whose provocative, Christopher Guest-style nonfiction film “American Theater” (except it’s a docu-, not mockumentary) is rolling out in select theaters now. A Slamdance Grand Jury Prize winner for documentary in 2025, the film is also executive-produced by Jeremy O. Harris.

“American Theater” follows Brian Clowdus — openly gay, conservative, and formerly of the Serenbe Playhouse in Georgia, who was taken down in 2019 over allegations of racism, misconduct, unsafe working conditions, and a gamut of other accusations. Clark and Frederick follow Clowdus, now a MAGA Republican, and a troupe of other conservative actors to an abandoned cabin in middle-of-nowhere Georgia where Clowdus plots the ultimate revenge: a community musical theater retelling of, of course, the 1692 Salem witch trials, riffing on Arthur Miller’s “The Crucible” (which, published in 1953, isn’t yet in the public domain). “This film was about a really fucked-up figure and a person with really fucked-up politics,” Harris told IndieWire over the phone from Copenhagen, where the Tony nominee is rehearsing a new play. “When you have unwelcoming and fucked-up politics, or a person who has unwelcoming, fucked-up politics at the center of the art you’re making, it can feel like potentially you’re endorsing their politics or celebrating them, especially because we don’t live in times that are deeply discursive or critical. In taking on someone who was once a formidable presence in the Southern regional theater space, Harris said the filmmakers saw “this opportunity to embed themselves in the company for his comeback show. They realized there was a chance to look at the type of fringe character that utilized MAGA for the grifting machine that it is. MAGA is a magnet for a lot of displaced people, and theater has so many displaced people. Even thinking about the fact that one of the most famous people that stormed the Capitol was in the regional production of ‘Jesus Christ Superstar’ meant that there were ways in which the theater community wasn’t looking at some of the foxes among the lambs in our own community. This gave them the opportunity to be those foxes, or not even foxes, but to be flies on the wall of this maker who was exploiting a lot of displaced people.”

A recent Cobble Hill Cinemas screening of “American Theater” was moderated by journalist Ludwig Hurtado. Next up, the film will be available to rent on the Letterboxd Video Store, so locally driven screenings also aim to bring audiences to that platform.

“One of the things that’s very sad to me is that amongst the distributors, the ones that one would think have the most bandwidth and power to really uplift these microbudget filmmakers who are truly keeping the torch burning for that independent American brio that put American independent cinema on the map and right next to so many other stalwarts of world cinema, a lot of them are being, I think, more cautious about who they’re distributing,” Harris said. “Distribution costs are so large right now that I think that they don’t really know what to do with movies so small. And so Letterboxd has become this really great outlet because there’s such a vibrant community there who are just excited to see films and excited to learn that filmmakers who maybe are in circumstances similar to their own as movie watchers are making films.”

In a separate statement, Frederick said, “The film takes place in 2021, when Trump was facing the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison, his political future was uncertain, and conservatives were batching DeSantis ‘24 tank tops. Democrats just had the best night of their lives in the midterms, and MAGA folks may find themselves at a low point, but it’s useful to remember that we’ve actually been here before.”

Clark added, “There was a moment when many people assumed the Trump era had come to an end. ‘American Theater’ tells a story of the Trump supporters during that time who were dedicated to figuring out what would come next. In this instance, their idea was an allegorical cancel culture musical about the Salem witch trials. It did not go anywhere near as planned, and our movie tells that story. But ultimately, everything that has happened to us as a nation ever since has only recontextualized what we saw within this brief moment in time.”

#3483. Sylvester Stallone Officially Wants a Former Spider-Man To Join Taylor Sheridan’s ‘Tulsa King’

At some point we might want to crown, unanimously I might add, Taylor Sheridan as the undisputed king of television. After penning the screenplay for Sicario, a 2015 action-crime thriller directed by Denis Villeneuve, Sheridan would return a few years later in monstrous fashion. Yellowstone arrived in 2018 and, with Kevin Costner at the fore, Sheridan was able to develop a neo-Western masterpiece that helped launch his own television empire.

Impressively, Sheridan's shows typically operate independently of one another. While his Yellowstone universe, which consists of prequels 1883 and 1923, as well as its sequels in Marshals and Dutton Ranch, maintain lots of connections because of the family links. Other Sheridan projects maintain an independence that is a testament to the quality of the individual stories and not a shared universe. The Madison, Lioness, Mayor of Kingstown, Landman are all distinct shows with deep, enthralling worlds that open up to audiences the more time they spend with the expertly crafted characters within. Sheridan has spent the best part of a decade transforming Paramount+ into the home of intense dramas. In October 2026, Sheridan had four shows securing spots on Amazon Store’s Top TV Shows charts.

However, Sheridan's television empire would not be complete without one of its prized jewels — Tulsa King. Starring Sylvester Stallone in its lead role, the series follows Stallone's Dwight "The General" Manfredi, a New York Mafia capo released from prison after 25 years who has taken up residence in Tulsa to build his criminal/legal empire. In his time in the Birthplace of Route 66, Stallone's Manfredi has seen off quite a number of villains and the Rocky star has ideas for an entirely new villain. Per Entertainment Weekly, Stallone discussed unexpectedly vibing with Oscar nominee, Andrew Garfield and how he'd fit into his Paramount+ crime series:

“I was with Andrew Garfield last night. I never thought we would hit it off, ever. I thought, boy, I’d love to have him as a villain in Tulsa King because it would create a whole different dynamic.”

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

In the very first season of Tulsa King, upon his release from prison, Manfredi faces off with Caolan Waltrip (Ritchie Coster), the leader of the Black Macadams outlaw motorcycle gang. After already being handed a lesson in betrayal by Don Charles "Chickie" Invernizzi (Domenick Lombardozzi), the son of Manfredi's New York boss in Season 1, Chickie resurfaces in Season 2 alongside Bill Bevilaqua (Frank Grillo), the head of the Kansas City mob, Cal Thresher (Neal McDonough), a wealthy, ruthless local businessman and his partner, Jackie Ming (Rich Ting). By Season 3, Jackie, Chickie, and Waltrip were already out of the picture. Bevilaqua and Thresher had both become Manfredi's allies of a sort, even as Jeremiah Dunmire (played by Robert Patrick) emerged as a new local threat and Ray "Quiet Ray" Renzetti (James Russo) as the latest New York-based villain.

Stallone has a unique idea of what sort of villain he wants Garfield to play in Tulsa King. “Instead of this big, lumbering, you know, villain, maybe it’s, you know, it’s thoughtful,” Stallone said. “Maybe it’s AI-driven. Maybe it’s something that I have no idea how to stop.”

Check out new episodes of Tulsa King every Friday on Paramount+ and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Taylor Sheridan’s future projects.

#3482. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Alleged Spying Scandal

The longtime Nvidia boss will be replaced with the company's Executive Vice president

After a month of headlines about an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang has stepped down from his leadership position at the AI chip company. Nvidia announced the decision on Thursday morning in a press release that described the company's next steps. Replacing Huang is Colette Kress, the current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA. Kress will be serving in an interim capacity until Nvidia finds a permanent successor.

Within video games, Nvidia is known as the company that powers computer graphics chips that make PC gaming possible. At large, Nvidia designs and is responsible for the vast majority of computer chips used for artificial intelligence. Nvidia's products are highly in-demand, which has led to an increase in gaming console prices across the board. Thanks to the AI boom, Nvidia and its multi-trillion dollar valuation have made it one of the biggest and most important companies in the world.

Nvidia was originally founded by Jensen in 1993, and the executive has been central to the company's public identity ever since. Back in October 2026, Huang was reported to be at the center of a Chinese spy plot. According to the New York Times, an intelligence asset named Alice Huang developed a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO with the apparent intention of directing more of the company's computer chips to China. The intelligence asset also reportedly sent back information she learned back to China. The tech mogul has since been accused of having an affair with another executive who reported directly to him — an act that violated Nvidia's code of conduct.

Though these are matters involving Huang's personal life, his position in the world of AI — and the government's agenda to strip China of any potential tech advantage — have made the affair a matter of national security. Beyond his position at Nvidia, Huang is considered a close ally of President Donald Trump.

Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board. Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

The year 2027 marks the original Star Wars movie's 50th anniversary, and Disney and Lucasfilm are celebrating the franchise's massive milestone in style with a variety of new immersive releases, toy collections, and brand partnerships. The experience will be played on the center of Cosm's 12k+ LED Dome in the film's original 16:9 format, with the Dome's surrounding projections "dynamically evolving" to further immerse audiences in the classic Star Wars locations and sequences.

#3480. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3479. ‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

Maybe you’re the kind of person who thinks about the first 10 minutes of “Up” from time to time, and wishes there was a film out there that would emotionally break you like that again. Maybe you long for less-processed-looking Minionesque animation and more painterly, natural worlds that find as much beauty in negative space as in color. Maybe it’s been a minute since “Flow,” and you would like a protagonist to hang out with another very good animated dog.

If your answer to any of the above is “yes,” then IndieWire has good news for you. The Annecy and Cannes Un Certain Regard Special Jury Prize-winning film “Iron Boy” is coming to U.S. theaters for a one-week awards-qualifying run in December, then launching in select cities on January 22, 2027. Writer/director Louis Clichy is a veteran of Pixar’s most undefeated run of films, including “Wall-E” and “Up,” as well as two fantastical “Asterix” adventures in France. With “Iron Boy,” he shows how big a seemingly small story can feel. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

Young farmboy Christophe starts tilting his head unintentionally, which eventually leads to a scoliosis diagnosis and an iron corset he has to wear everywhere. But, of course, his spine is far from the only thing out of alignment in Christophe’s life — straightening those emotions and ambitions out, discovering who he wants to be, is the real journey. But it’s one that occasionally turns its entire watercolor world sideways like the most beautiful magical realist snowglobe you’ve ever seen.

It’s one that, as Rafael Motomayor said in IndieWire’s review, “makes ‘Iron Boy’ stand out even amongst European animated films. The film employs mostly non-professional voice actors, including Clinchy’s own son (who plays Christophe), and the director would often record the lines on location, to give the performances a less constructed sound than if they were done in the clear confines of a studio. It makes the story feel quasi-documentary in its approach, an intimate and deeply personal story of a boy searching for more than what life has offered him, restrained by a physical affliction that nevertheless allows him to live an extraordinary life.”

#3478. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3476. Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards

The Film Independent Spirit Awards are returning to the Hollywood Palladium with a new pair of hosts in tow.

Film Independent, the nonprofit organization dedicated to championing independent storytelling and supporting artists, announced on Wednesday, December 10 that “Maddie’s Secret” stars Kate Berlant and John Early will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards.

The acclaimed comedians, actors and longtime creative collaborators, who have written and/or starred together in other projects like Emmy-nominated variety special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” and cult comedy series “Search Party” will bring their comedic sensibilities to the 42nd annual Spirit Awards. The celebration of the best in independent film and television takes place Saturday, March 6, 2027 in Los Angeles, California. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

“If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” said Juan Devis, President of Film Independent, as part of the announcement. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. The Nominee Brunch, an annual highlight honoring all nominees and featuring the presentation of the Emerging Filmmaker Awards, will take place on Saturday, January 9, 2027 at The London West Hollywood.

Berlant and Early join a roster of past Spirit Awards hosts that includes Ego Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg, and John Waters.

#3475. Jessica Chastain Confirms Surprising Prediction About Christopher Nolan’s Interstellar

EXCLUSIVE: Jessica Chastain recalls working with Christopher Nolan on the set of Interstellar.

When Interstellar debuted in 2014, critics and audiences gave it mixed reviews; they were impressed by its stunning, groundbreaking visuals but weren't sold on its melodramatic tone and heavy-handed exposition. However, the divisive reception didn't last long, as the thriller ultimately became one of Nolan's most celebrated movies to date. The movie stood the test of time, with viewers learning to appreciate its emotional significance. Interstellar's continued streaming success also massively contributed to its shifting public reception, transforming it from a polarizing film to a beloved sci-fi classic.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Liam Crowley, Chastain, who played adult Murphy in Interstellar, shared that she knew the 2014 movie would be a timeless classiclike Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey. Even though shooting the film “felt like a small movie,” Chastain predicted that they were making something special. The Academy Award winner also recalled telling Nolan during production that Interstellar was definitely a movie ahead of its time.

Jessica Chastain: It was just a quiet, peaceful, zen-like set. I remember it felt like a small movie; even though it wasn't a small movie, it felt very intimate. And Chris was so respectful of the actors, and he was very careful and deliberate with his words and protective. I mean, one thing that people don't understand is that when Interstellar came out, it was not a success. People didn't get it. And I said to Chris at the time when 2001: A Space Odyssey came out, the New York Times called it immensely boring. And that is a film that has withstood the test of time. And I said, "Interstellar is made before its time." And little did I know, 10 years later, I think it's one of the greatest films in his canon, and that's pretty impressive because he has incredible films, but it goes to show sometimes you make something and people don't get it. But the wonderful thing about film and storytelling is that you don't know when it's going to hit, but it's going to affect people, and it withstands the test of time.

In Interstellar, Chastain played the adult version of Murphy Cooper, the daughter of Matthew McConaughey's character, who grew up to become a top NASA scientist. She had a significant role in saving humanity from its dying planet by making a scientific breakthrough that allowed NASA to build space stations where people could evacuate to.

Following the film's release, while critics praised Chastain's performance as the story's emotional anchor, some felt that the acclaimed actor was underutilized. She also shared the role with Mackenzie Foy as 10-year-old Murphy and Ellen Burstyn as the elderly Murphy.

Interstellar takes place in a dystopian future where humanity faces a life-threatening famine because of Earth's dying ecosystem. To solve this crisis, NASA sends a small team of astronauts on a deep-space mission in search of a potential new home for humanity. Following its initial theatrical run and subsequent IMAX re-releases, the 2014 movie has already grossed over $782 million worldwide. It also currently holds a Fresh rating of 73% on Rotten Tomatoes, while its audience score is higher at 87%.

#3474. George R. R. Martin Officially Picks Dunk & Egg Over ‘Winds of Winter’

Waiting for George R. R. Martin to finish The Winds of Winter has become something of a tradition for Game of Thrones fans. It's been more than 15 years since A Dance with Dragons arrived in bookstores, and despite countless updates, the sixth installment of A Song of Ice and Fire still doesn't have a release date. That hasn't stopped Martin from expanding Westeros elsewhere, of course, with House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms introducing audiences to different generations of the Seven Kingdoms. And it turns out the author has been spending some of his time working on another story that should make fans of the latter particularly happy.

Martin is officially working on a fourth Dunk and Egg novella, according to A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms showrunner Ira Parker, even as fans continue waiting for The Winds of Winter. Speaking with THR, Parker confirmed that Martin has been developing another adventure featuring Ser Duncan the Tall and his young squire, Egg.

Book four, which George is working on, takes place in a very cool location.

Although Parker didn't identify the setting, Martin previously revealed that the fourth novella would take place at Winterfell. In a 2014 blog post, he explained that the story would involve a collection of formidable Stark women known as the She-Wolves of Winterfell.

The news also arrives as HBO continues developing A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, which stars Peter Claffey (Bad Sisters) as Ser Duncan the Tall and Dexter Sol Ansell (The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes) as Egg. Parker has also said that it's the aim of the production team to follow the characters across several stages of their lives, potentially allowing the younger cast members to age naturally, so they don't need to recast. Which is only fair, because Ansell is wonderful in his role as Egg.

Five is the last story point of Egg as a boy. So it's a very natural ending place for us to take a break and come back when Dexter is older. So then we can do Egg the Prince, do some politics, do some fun stuff in Summerhall and King's Landing, and get a different vibe where they're not on the road all the time. So if the show wraps and people are still OK with everything we're doing and there's still an appetite, let the show evolve along with our leads, with myself and with the rest of our creative team as we grow older and the world changes and we want to say different things. I think that would be a lovely way to tell a story about these two guys through the course of their lives.

And when asked whether he would consider recasting Egg with an older performer, Parker made his preference clear. "No. Dexter is our Egg. Or, at least, Dexter is my Egg — I have no controlling interest in this property. But Dexter and Peter are my guys."

The first season of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is streaming on HBO Max, with Season 2 expected in the first half of 2027. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is based on George R. R. Martin's Tales of Dunk and Egg novellas and is set around 100 years before the events of Game of Thrones. It follows Ser Duncan the Tall and his squire, Egg, who would later become King Aegon V Targaryen.

#3473. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3472. ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 16, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

It’s the final weekend of summer in 1986, upwardly aspirant Jewish families across Queens are still crowding around country club pools to make sure they get their annual money’s worth, and — in a little less than two months — the Mets are going to win the World Series for what might be the last time in team history. But nebbishy engineer Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) doesn’t know that yet. He doesn’t know that this is his golden age. He doesn’t know that this is as good as it’s ever going to get.  Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

What Irwin knows is that greed is good. That the income gap is widening at an unprecedented rate, that economic mobility is slowing to a crawl, and that his giant older brother Gary (Adam Driver) — a divorced ex-police officer who swans around the city like a majestic bird in a blue Mercedes — has started to make him feel even smaller than usual. What Irwin knows is that his mother-in-law wants him to move the family to Great Neck, that the older of his two bickering teenage sons wants an expensive party for his 18th birthday, and that his beautiful wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) wants fewer things to worry about. Irwin isn’t the overly ambitious sort, but a man can only live in the suburbs of Mt. Olympus for so long before it starts to feel like the gods are taunting him to claim a small piece of it for himself.

And so the stage is set for James Gray’s deft and devastating “Paper Tiger,” a Jewish-American tragedy in a teapot that — like all of the writer/director’s best films — is both sweepingly mythic and hauntingly personal all at once. That double effect, once a magic trick that Gray’s movies would manage to pull off by the time they ended, has since become the de facto starting condition of his singular auto-cinema, which continues to pick at his formative wounds by processing them through the classics.

As indebted to Aeschylus as “Ad Astra” was to Joseph Campbell, or “The Lost City of Z” was to Henri Rousseau, “Paper Tiger” begins with a telling quote from the ancient playwright’s most famous text: “Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.” Even more telling, however, is the opening shot that follows, which surveys the same reedy marshland — or at least one identical to it — from the end of “We Own the Night.” It’s no surprise that a project first conceived as a direct sequel to 2022’s “Armageddon Time” should point back to Gray’s previous work, but never before has it been so clear, so fast, that he’s trying to process his own, highly specific experience by assimilating it into the curriculum that first taught him how to make sense of the world. The more acutely self-referential his films get, the more broadly they speak to the soft and immortal agony that propels their characters forward.

It’s an agony that goes by many (sur)names, but is colloquially referred to as “family.” “Paper Tiger” is many things, chief among them a textbook parable about the American Dream, a breathless thriller about a working-class schmuck who gets mixed up with the Russian mafiya, and a pleasantly open question about why Miles Teller has rededicated his career to cosplaying as “Lost in America”-era Albert Brooks (to my mind, a canny, convincing way of aging up the nonconformist spunk that first defined his screen image in the days of “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now”). But, at its most nuclear level, “Paper Tiger” is — to an even more explicit degree than “Little Odessa,” “The Yards,” and any of the other James Gray movies that it hungrily mulches into something all its own — a remarkably knowing and perceptive film about how family is, and has always been, the ultimate devil’s bargain. Our greatest strength and our heaviest cross to bear. The reason our most dangerous risks can seem worth taking, and the most valuable thing we risk by taking them.

Irwin gives “Paper Tiger” its shape, but it’s how Gary navigates those dilemmas that gives the film its soul. Heartbreakingly portrayed by Adam Driver in a career-best performance that stretches across flash, menace, and pure sincerity like a foot stepping down on a bed of nails without drawing blood, Gary is a vintage ’80s showboat who only knows how to show affection by offering to share in his apparent success. He strides into Irwin and Hester’s living room — after months of radio silence — with the razzle dazzle of a local celebrity and a fully catered feast from Peter Luger’s Steak House in tow for good measure. Irwin’s sons marvel at the gun their uncle still keeps holstered around his ankle (cool!), and his wide-eyed wife looks across the kitchen table and imagines what her life might have been like had she held out for the shinier Pearl.

At least, that’s what Irwin seems to imagine that his wife is imagining, though he’d sooner let such fears fester inside of him for the rest of his natural life than to speak them aloud. For all of the character’s frustrated aspirations for a better life, Teller endows him with the wizened humility of a second-generation Jewish immigrant who knows that it would be gauche to forsake what his late father-in-law — tempting to picture as Anthony Hopkins for continuity’s sake — sacrificed to make possible for their family. Irwin might even be smart enough to recognize that his brother is an empty promise in a tailored suit, but, in a less literal expression of the double vision that will soon cause his wife to crash her car into a tree, being smart isn’t the same as seeing things clearly.

Whatever the case, Irwin is powerless to resist his brother’s sales pitch when Gary lures him into the basement to reveal the reason purpose of his visit: An ambitious new business venture is seeping its way into the Gowanus Canal, and it could use a sharp engineer to help facilitate their plans for the waterway. Still connected to the gills after getting rich in the private sector, Gary doesn’t tell his naive kid brother that said venture is the Russian mob, but the beauty of it is that he doesn’t have to. It can just be another one of the many different things that Irwin doesn’t know. He’ll go down there, sketch a few diagrams for some bald and scary men straight out of central casting, and take home a healthy paycheck to his family (“Paper Tiger” won’t score any points for bucking mafia stereotypes, as Gray plays up their ruthlessness in order to stress how far Irwin is out of his depth).

The only problem is that Irwin takes the job as seriously as he would any other, and — to his profound regret — takes his two sons to go scope out the canal one night, where they see the Russians illegally dumping their waste into the water. The Russians don’t like that. They don’t know what he’s doing there. And, in the aftermath of a stomach-churning stick-up that twisted my guts with the queasy horror of a repressed memory, Gary is given a week to make the problem go away. Spoiler alert: Appeasing the leader of an organized crime ring isn’t as simple as cutting a check, and wouldn’t be even if Gary had access to $125,000.

It doesn’t take long for things to spiral out of control from there, as Irwin and his boys soon find themselves in the crosshairs of a turf war they are comically ill-prepared to survive, while Hester — kept in the dark for her own protection — is thrust into a different crucible that she chooses to keep secret from her husband for similar reasons. (Despite being heavily affected by period drag, Johansson’s performance is too limpid to be mistaken for caricature, growing more hollowed out and heartsick with every scene until it assumes the same void-like power that Brad Pitt once found in the farthest reaches of outer space.) Plotted with a fatalistic velocity that would make Aeschylus proud, Gray’s script corkscrews towards ruin at a sickening pace, its slick road to hell paved with a well-textured mixture of imperfect intentions.

For all of the red meat that “Paper Tiger” gets to chew off the bone, this is still a small and maybe slightly underfunded movie, its outsized impact only made possible because of the micro-details that Gray traces within and between his characters. And I’m not talking about the assortment of beepers and TaB cans, or the load-bearing shots of ’80s New York, which are all Joaquín Baca-Asay’s 35mm cinematography needs to complete the illusion of time travel. While the film is buttressed by a handful of exquisite setpieces (including a nightmarish home invasion sequence that transposes the film’s title into a piece of shadowplay, and a climactic shoutout that binds it even closer to the rest of Gray’s body of work), it’s ultimately fueled by the atomic frictions inside Driver’s performance.

To that point, the real tragedy of “Paper Tiger” isn’t that messing with the mob tears these brothers apart, but rather that it brings them together. There’s not a lot of time for fun and games, but it’s never lost on Gray that this is the most time Gary and Irwin have spent with each other in years — maybe even since they were kids. “We’ve never played in the dirt,” Gary tells Irwin as he lies to his brother about how everything  about the Gowanus deal is above board. But they’re playing together now. The worse things get, the more they expose the extraordinary bond that allowed things to get so fucked up in the first place (a dynamic that becomes all the more wrenching because of how Gray transposes it onto Irwin’s sons). The worse things get, the more this movie sympathizes with Gary and Irwin for their parts in it.

It’s not that Gary is trying to do something nice for his brother, or that he’s shamelessly using Irwin to broker a lucrative deal with the Russians, but rather that everything that happens after that fateful offer stems from an inextricable braid of love and leverage. Gray is no stranger to saga about fraternal strains, but never has he so forcefully tugged at the ties that bind, or more sensitively observed how they can suffocate an entire family when a certain force pulls on them hard enough.

“Paper Tiger” is a story about a household gripped by a self-inflicted event that chokes the life out of its lungs, and precious few films have better conveyed what it feels like when the oxygen gets sucked out of a home without any hope of coming back. “We already had everything,” Irwin will eventually mutter under his breath. The deepest cut of this unshakeable tragedy is that, for the very first time, it leaves him begging for more.

“Paper Tiger” premiered in Competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. NEON will release it in theaters later this year.

#3471. I’m a Deals Writer, and These Are My Top 10 Tech Deals This Week

As Lifehacker's deals writer, I'm always looking for the best bargains on TVs, speakers, laptops, and other tech. Now that it's Friday, I've gathered together this week's sales highlights, all of which I've vetted using my favorite price-tracking tools to make sure they are actually good deals.

This week, you can already feel the early Black Friday deals heating up with price cuts on the M5 MacBook Air, Bose speakers and headphones, a Samsung OLED TV, and more.

The MacBook Air with the M5 chip comes in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: Amazon is selling both right now at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The WH-1000XM5 headphones were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6s. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99). These are still incredible headphones in 2026, and with a $200 discount, they are a steal.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case.

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269). This is a great opportunity to snatch a quality portable speaker with a big discount.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade.

The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179), the lowest price they've ever been. They use the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0.

I got the Roborock Qrevo CurvX because it seemed like the perfect robot vacuum for me, as I have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, and it excels at handling them all. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been.

Samsung’s HW-Q600F soundbar is down to $379.97 at Amazon from $499.99, a $110 discount that brings it to its lowest price ever. This 2025 model sits in the middle of Samsung’s Q-Series lineup and pairs a sleek, angular bar with a subwoofer in a 3.1.2 setup. Dolby Atmos also brings a modest sense of height, and effects track cleanly from left to right. You get a graphic equalizer and sound presets for adjusting the audio to your preferences through the included remote.

The Ultimate Ears Miniroll is down to $49.99 (originally $79.99), the second-lowest it has sold for so far. It’s a small, flat, puck-shaped Bluetooth speaker that weighs just over half a pound, with a removable rubber strap you can attach to a backpack, bike handlebar, or shower caddy. Despite its size, the Miniroll can get surprisingly loud—which PCMag confirms in its review—and at moderate volume, it has enough sound for a kitchen or backyard without sounding thin. As for its battery life, you get about 12 hours of playback before it needs a charge over USB-C, while its IP67 rating protects it from dust and a brief dunk in water.

#3470. DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues

When they were hired to run DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran were tasked with turning the struggling comic book company into a true rival to Marvel. Four years later, the two have been handed their walking papers before they were able to accomplish their task.

Skydance, which recently bought Warner Bros. Discovery and with it the rights to heroes like Superman, Batman, and the other DC staples that Gunn and Safran were trying to reinvigorate, opted to go in another, cheaper direction. They brought in Jeremy Latcham, a low-profile executive who, like Gunn, had spent years working for Marvel, to oversee DC’s latest reboot. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

There have been mutterings that the change was because of the commercial performance of DC’s films, and the track record has been a mixed bag. “Superman” did what it needed to do, earning $618.7 million worldwide on a $225 million budget, but it wasn’t a blockbuster on the level of Christopher Nolan’s “Dark Knight” films or “Aquaman.”

But “Supergirl” was an unmitigated disaster, earning $126.5 million against a $170 million budget, resulting in losses of roughly $100 million. And “Clayface,” a body horror film produced for $44 million, has been a modest success, earning approximately $110 million. So no, Gunn and Safran had yet to produce a “Guardians of the Galaxy”-style smash that taps the zeitgeist. Though, to be fair, Marvel hasn’t made as many of those lately either. Tastes have changed, and comic book movies, at least ones not starring Spider-Man, aren’t as popular as they once were.

But look closer, and Gunn and Safran’s ouster is about something more than their films’ commercial performances. It’s about cost-cutting too, something that Skydance, with its $80 billion in net debt, needs to start chipping away at if it’s going to realize the $6 billion in savings it’s promised to find.

The duo’s deal, which was set to expire in 2027, was unusually generous. Safran not only got paid to run the comic book label, he was also allowed to run The Safran Company, the wildly successful production company behind “The Conjuring” franchise (former Netflix film chief Dan Lin, in contrast, divested from his company Rideback when he went over to the streamer). Then there was Gunn, who commanded fees for producing films like “Supergirl” and “Clayface,” as well as fees for those DC films that he wrote and directed, such as “Superman” and “Man of Tomorrow.” Gunn’s total haul for a DC film could be as high as $10 million for all his various duties, according to insiders.

When Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav offered the pair such a sweet deal, comic book movies looked more durable and he needed to make a splash after DC produced flops like “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom” and “The Flash.” To sweeten the offer, Zaslav also allowed Gunn and Safran to be relatively autonomous, reporting directly to him, whereas Skydance wanted the DC leadership to be under Skydance Motion Picture Group chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein.

Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.’ film unit since taking over. The studio has suffered a devastating wave of flops this year, losing hundreds of millions on a slate that included bombs such as “Digger,” “The Bride!,” and last weekend’s “The Cat in the Hat.” One insider put the estimated losses at nearing $1 billion. Of course, most of those films were greenlit under Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy, who were let go as soon as David Ellison got the keys to the Warner lot, and have nothing to do with Gunn or Safran. But it does put pressure on Skydance to turn things around and improve the film division’s margins, fast. On an earnings call this week, Ellison acknowledged the film division faces “headwinds” and “has underperformed this year.” He went on to pledge to “apply the same playbook we did at Paramount: greenlighting more selectively.”

Safran remains widely respected on the lot for his stewardship of DC, and is praised for trying to keep budgets in line and for cleaning up the company’s byzantine production practices so that its films, shows, and comic books had a unifying creative voice. Gunn, though a gifted filmmaker, had a harder time adjusting to life in the c-suite, something he admitted to this week in a lengthy post on X. “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.” He closed by saying that he was excited to return to working purely as a creator.

Gunn’s habit of engaging with fans directly on social media raised eyebrows at Warner Bros. and, later, at Skydance. But it cut both ways, with Gunn often using his vast following to promote upcoming projects and to engage more directly with fans in a way that inspired loyalty. Insiders also credit Safran and Gunn with not only reinvigorating Superman on screen, but also backing critically acclaimed shows such as “Lanterns” and “Peacemaker.” And the pair handled a delicate situation with the production of “The Batman: Part II,” which was delayed because of personal issues involving its writer and director Matt Reeves, a situation that ultimately required Steven Soderbergh to step in to finish the sequel under Reeves’ guidance. It is expected to wrap production in the next few weeks.

Insiders also note that Gunn and Safran didn’t have a chance to fully realize their vision of making superhero films featuring a wider variety of characters across a greater diversity of genres made for a broader range of budgets. Gunn was already plotting his next move even as he edited “Man of Tomorrow,” which features a team-up of Lex Luthor and Superman. He had outlined a third “Superman” film and was working on a “Justice League” and a “Batman” film, either one of which was expected to be his next project.

In Hollywood, however, timing is everything. And Gunn and Safran had the misfortune of trying to build their own MCU just as comic book movies were declining in popularity. Will Latcham have more success? He’s widely liked and boasts ties to the Christian community that could broaden DC’s core audience. But he also doesn’t come with the kind of pedigree and profile that Gunn did.

As for DC’s fans, they are bracing for yet another reboot having seen the comic book brand they love go through three different regimes over the last decade. Will Latcham provide the kind of consistency the company so desperately needs, or will he be just the latest in a long line of executives asked to pull off a miracle without being granted much of a runway?
