#3469. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3468. The 10 Most Uplifting Romance Movies of All Time, Ranked

There are undeniably sappy romantic movies out there, and sure, some of them are nice when you're in the mood for that kind of thing. On the other end of things, you’ve also got downbeat romantic movies, or films that might well be anti-romances. Break-up movies would fit into this category (see Blue Valentine, Scenes from a Marriage, and Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind).

If you want something that doesn’t feel sappy, though, yet you're also not in the mood to have your soul crushed, the movies below might well be worth jumping into. They are the best uplifting romance movies ever made, because they go for some big emotional beats without overdoing it, and really, what they’re all going for tonally is just nailed. That’s the main thing, and yes, most of them can be recommended to grouchy people who might be tempted to write off all romance movies as too cheesy or sentimental. These ones could make those folks see the light.

Amélie is a nice movie that’s also largely about being nice. That’s what the titular character does, and sure, she’s a bit eccentric and maybe a tad unsettling, but she is nice. She means well. And also, the world around her is pretty strange and definitely heightened, so she kind of fits in with that world, albeit not perfectly, but again, she’s trying, and she wants to find someone she can fall in love with, too.

There aren’t a ton of narrative beats here, so Amélie is technically light on story, yet that doesn’t matter too much when it’s going for something else, and because it wants to be more than a little strange throughout and stuff. Also, Amélie looks pretty great throughout, with a bold use of color and an overall energy that makes it feel quite fantastical at times, alongside the unusual sense of humor and the quirky romance angle it has going on at the same time, too.

Bill Murray plays the main character in Groundhog Day, and that guy, Phil, is a pretty rotten one at the start of the movie. He’s then put through hell, though, because he keeps living the same tedious day over and over again, which feels like karma for a while, but then goes on long enough that you start feeling sorry for him and hope he can break out of it.

And, like, he does, because Groundhog Day is here among uplifting movies, so that does guarantee it has at least a somewhat nice ending. It’s well-earned, thankfully, and it does make for a pretty substantial and undeniably great character arc. Elsewhere, Groundhog Day balances all the genres it belongs to (comedy, romance, fantasy to some extent, and a little by way of drama) incredibly well.

The Big Sick isn't just based on a true story, but one of the people in that true story, Kumail Nanjiani, pretty much plays himself. He was also a writer, alongside Emily V. Gordon, with Nanjiani and Gordon being married in real life, and The Big Sick is loosely based on what happened when they met, fell in love, and then navigated Gordon (named Emily Gardner in the film) being diagnosed with Still's disease.

Because it touches upon that, it’s kind of a romantic dramedy, but when you know it was written by two people who are still together, a happy ending is inevitable, with it just being the case that they have to go through a lot before that sense of emotional catharsis is reached. As a film, The Big Sick feels very sincere, and the ups and downs of the whole situation are felt immensely throughout.

Sure, Punch-Drunk Love is a romance movie that’s heavy on anxiety, so it’s not really an easy watch, but it does end up being heartwarming, at least once you battle past all the nerves. That’s what the main character has to do, kind of. Like, he endures a lot before he can eventually be in love with someone else out there who complements his personality while sharing some of his struggles.

Paul Thomas Anderson is at his most sentimental here, and yeah, that’s not saying a lot, since he’s not exactly the most sentimental of directors, but what he tries to do here? He does make it work. Also, Adam Sandler really is fantastic in Punch-Drunk Love, playing a huge role in the tense part of the movie feeling as tense as it does while also making his character, Barry Egan, feel sympathetic alongside feeling flawed.

While it isn't quite old enough to be a classic just yet, there’s a good chance Sing Street will be considered one once enough time has passed. For now, it’s still tentatively worth considering as an all-time great musical, and of all the movies and TV shows from the 2010s that looked back upon the 1980s in one way or another, this is absolutely one of the better ones.

It’s about a teenage boy navigating a strained home life and some difficult times at a new school, and then what happens when he decides to put together a band basically only because he wants to impress a girl. There are so many points in Sing Street where it could've felt like too much, or become a bit too cheesy, but it toes the line perfectly and is ultimately very sweet without being saccharine.

It isn’t the most twee of all the Wes Anderson films, but Moonrise Kingdom does still have its moments, and it’s unlikely anyone will mistake it for the work of another director. It's set on a small island and follows two 12-year-olds who fall in love and decide to run away together. When they venture into the wilderness, they prove capable of surviving, but some adults still band together and try to find them.

It’s got a good mix of coming-of-age stuff, comedy, and romance that ultimately feels quite sweet. Moonrise Kingdom gets a bit overshadowed by The Grand Budapest Hotel, which came out a couple of years later and seems to be regarded by most people as the better Wes Anderson movie, but Moonrise Kingdom should still be allowed to stand on its own, and out of any other movie’s shadow. It’s also a good balance between the hyper-Wes Anderson movies (2014 onwards) and the stuff from the 1990s and 2000s that felt ever so slightly more grounded and, for lack of a better word, authentic.

If you can find a person who doesn’t like The Princess Bride, then congrats, because you’ve found the human being equivalent of a diamond (in terms of rareness… maybe not in terms of other qualities associated with diamonds). Here, you get a movie that feels like a fairy tale and a gentle parody of those sorts of stories at the same time, and then it’s also a story within a story, which is a way to reflect the postmodern quality of the book the movie was based on.

It all works quite miraculously, and even judged generally as a movie, rather than a comedic romance/fantasy film, it really could well be one of the very best of all time.

Still, it’s a fairly different movie compared to the book, in some ways, and maybe has a tiny bit more heart in the end? It all works quite miraculously, and even judged generally as a movie, rather than a comedic romance/fantasy film, it really could well be one of the very best of all time. It’s one of the most uplifting and pleasing of all the crowd-pleasers.

Singin’ in the Rain is possibly the best of all the classic musicals, and also likely the easiest to get into and appreciate. It’s got a breezy story about the film industry transitioning from silent movies to talkies, and while you get a sense of the difficulties involved with all that, it never becomes a heavy-going or downbeat watch. If you want something thematically similar, but more cynical and/or darkly comedic, there is always Sunset Boulevard and the more recent Babylon.

There’s also a chance Singin’ in the Rain is great and irresistible enough to convert someone who might otherwise be a musical naysayer. There’s a focus on comedy here, above all else, and then some simple but sweet romance thrown in for good measure, so yes, it can still count here for present purposes. It’s just a good time of a movie, and one of the most undeniably likable in the history of cinema, too.

The Before trilogy is an undeniably fascinating one. The first movie, Before Sunrise, is probably the most romantic, make no mistake. That one sees two young people meeting by chance, spending a whole night together, and then having to part in the morning, saying they’ll reconnect, but not knowing if that'll really come to pass. It does come to pass, but only nine years later, and by chance, in Before Sunset.

They only spend a bit over an hour together in this one, and there are more realities of life explored here that stop it from feeling as sweeping or consistently romantic as Before Sunrise. Yet the reconnecting happening at all – and the ultimately hopeful final scene – do make it eventually feel like the most optimistic film of the three (and then the final one, Before Midnight, is more grounded and intense, yet still a great way to round out the whole trilogy).

You might not like rom-coms generally, but When Harry Met Sally is so good you'll probably be willing to make an exception for it. Well, if you don’t make an exception for it, then you're missing out, since it is effortlessly funny and romantic without ever being contrived or running the risk of feeling cheesy. It’s just honest about relationships and the ups and downs of falling for someone, but then in the end, it focuses more on the ups.

The harder parts of navigating a long-term relationship make that ending more rewarding, of course, and this all sounds very obvious, but genuinely, no other romance movie of the sort that When Harry Met Sally is does it as well. Annie Hall is very well-written and honest, but somewhat more bittersweet by the end, while When Harry Met Sally is just all sweet by the end, yet thankfully not in a way that'll make you feel nauseous. It’s just a great movie.

#3467. Apple @ Work: Mac admins are shipping AI-written code with mistakes, but fixing the problems is taking days

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

There’s no doubt that AI tools are making IT admins faster at writing code, researching issues, etc. As a Mac admin, I’ve seen slow but steady growth in how I’ve used it in my daily work across all aspects of IT. It’s not perfect, though. I’ve used it to write scripts, troubleshoot networking errors, and more. A new report from Fleet puts numbers on the problem: it’s easy to ship things, but it’s hard to undo mistakes.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For this report, Fleet surveyed more than 250 enterprise IT folks who manage Apple, all with admin access to their device management systems. The folks responding to the survey manage an average of 2,000 devices, and nearly half have 6 to 10 years of Apple admin experience.

The debate over whether IT teams should use AI day-to-day is over. They already are, and in the past 30 days, 68% of those responding reported using AI for troubleshooting or log analysis, 62% used it to write scripts, and 61% used it to author device management profiles or configurations. The log analysis is something that I use AI for often. 86% allow AI-written output into production after some form of review, and only 14% keep it out of their production environments entirely. There simply is no world where IT can operate at the speed needed without AI tools.

69% of respondents can’t roll back a bad configuration change within an hour, and 43% need more than a day. Another 26% of those responding can recover the same day, but only by doing it by hand. This is the biggest red flag of the survey, in my opinion. AI lets you ship anything fast, but AI can ship bugs just like humans can.

Here’s a real scenario that can happen: an IT admin asks an AI assistant to write a configuration profile, takes a quick pass at it, and pushes it to a few thousand Macs in seconds. If something is wrong with it (a bad network setting, a restriction that locks people out of an app they need), unwinding it could take a while.

“Mac admins are basically engineers now, whether their job description calls them that or not.”

I agree with him, and I am somewhat not happy about it. The job of an Apple admin has moved a long way from deploying Macs and iPads and managing through a device management console. Today it’s identity, security, compliance, and app lifecycle, all on top of a macOS release that forces changes every year. IT teams keep getting more and more added to them without additional resources or taking things away.

31% said keeping up with Apple’s release cadence is their single biggest IT challenge, far ahead of everything else on the survey. On the bright side, Apple’s own management architecture is moving in the right direction. 53% already have declarative device management in production.

Apple has done a lot of work here, and it’s not even Apple that is to blame for the frustration. Apple has built the platform for IT to do everything it needs to do. It’s everything else. Security is harder. AI has made it harder. It’s the expectation that IT has to own AI while owning literally everything else.

IT is using AI to help with its work because it’s the only way to survive the onslaught of the AI era. You aren’t getting more help, but you’re expected to do more without anything being taken away from you. Even systems that don’t need as much day-to-day management as they did years ago, you still have to own and secure them. Hosted email is a good example here. Yes, 365 and Workspace have made it easier to keep email running. You aren’t managing servers as you did 20 years ago, but email is still not easy. You traded server management for AI-driven phishing scams, MFA management, and more. It’s two steps forward and one back. We need a period of three steps forward and zero back to get back to where IT needs to be.

You can read Fleet’s full Apple in the enterprise report on its website.

#3466. Harry Potter: Every Hogwarts Teacher, Ranked By Power

Harry Potter was undeniably taught by some of the powerful witches and wizards at Hogwarts, but they were far from equal. The Defense Against the Dark Arts teachers were particularly potent, simply because they had learned how to defeat some of the most dangerous magic in the world; even Professor Lockhart was skilled in his own way. Meanwhile, wizards like Professor Flitwick were known as skilled duelists.

But, of course, there's naturally a ranking of power—even among some of the greatest witches and wizards of the age. It's quite hard to judge some of Harry's teachers in terms of power level, because not all of them have demonstrated spectacular feats. The upcoming Harry Potter TV show will include scenes that aren't from the books, so may well give us more information; for now, though, the absence of those feats is in itself a useful indicator. Here are all Harry's Hogwarts teachers, ranked by power.

Note: I'm choosing to ignore the Carrows, who were never really accepted by the Hogwarts staff (or, I suspect, by Hogwarts itself). I'm also omitting a couple of teachers who we know next to nothing about, specifically Professors Kettleburn and Silvanus. I'm also choosing to ignore Hogwarts' support staff, such as Madam Pomfrey, Argus Filch, and Madam Hooch.

Let's start with the wizard who is surely the least powerful, because he never demonstrated any magic at all; Professor Binns, Hogwarts' only ghost teacher. The man is so boring, he gives you the impression he simply carried on teaching and never noticed he'd died. We don't actually know whether ghosts retain their past magical abilities, but it seems unlikely, and Professor Binns showed no power at all (or any interest in practical magic, for that matter). Little wonder students tended to fall asleep in History of Magic.

Most Hogwarts students believe Professor Sybil Trelawney to be a fraud, and Umbridge banished her as one. But Professor Trelawney does hail from the bloodline of powerful seers, and she's produced at least two disturbingly accurate prophesies—including the one that kicked off the entire Harry Potter saga. Dumbledore largely kept Professor Trelawney at Hogwarts for her own protection, because he knew how dangerous that prophecy really is.

We don't really know how skilled or powerful Bathsheba Babbling really is, because her topic wasn't really one that interested Harry; she was professor of Ancient Runes, which perhaps suggests a deep specialism. The Harry Potter stories largely ignore runes, so we get no sense of what she's capable of. That said, I'm choosing to single her out on this list because other specialists seem to be quite powerful. It may be this is one area of the Wizarding World that has been neglected.

The ill-fated Professor Burbage was Professor of Muggle Studies, until she was eventually targeted and killed by the Death Eaters. There's nothing to indicate her power levels, because it's certainly not a mark of weakness that she was captured and executed by Voldemort and his assembled Death Eaters. Still, the absence of feats is notable, and means she appears low on this list. Her last act was to appeal to Severus Snape for mercy.

Harry's first Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher, Professor Quirrell was considered impressive by Hagrid—but never really demonstrated why. Vain and ambitious, he traveled the world in search of Voldemort, and it's unknown whether he wanted the glory of capturing him or whether he wanted to learn from him. In either case, even a diminished and broken Voldemort was able to possess him, proving how weak Quirrell really is.

It's easy to underestimate Gilderoy Lockhart; Harry's Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher in his second year, he had traveled the world wiping memories and claiming the feats of other witches and wizards as his own. But this Memory Charm alone is a complex piece of magic, and he may well have been a magical powerhouse if he hadn't been so lazy. In the end, Lockhart was hoist by his own petard, his own memories erased by a backfiring broken wand.

The centaur Firenze taught Divination at Hogwarts after he was expelled from his people due to helping humans. He's perhaps the most intriguing character to place on this ranking, because wizards tended to think of centaurs as beneath them, and he certainly didn't possess the kind of magic we see with other professors. Still, centaurs are remarkable in their own right, not least due to their (disturbingly accurate) ability to read the stars. He's a skilled archer, and possesses remarkable physical strength. He may well also have a degree of resistance to magic, like other magical beings.

Professor Grubbly-Plank took over Care of Magical Creatures during Order of the Phoenix, and had the misfortune of being a competent teacher who was resented by Harry and his friends. Unlike Hagrid, she doesn't just have experience of magical creatures; she's also a witch in her own right, likely with a strong specialism. Given the field she operates in, it seems right to place her at this point in the rankings.

The Ministry of Magic appointed Dolores Umbridge as Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher during Harry's fifth year, and she's a difficult one to evaluate. Although she had a fearsome reputation, she excels at manipulation, so that's probably less reliable than it was with even Gilderoy Lockhart. She was competent at Transfiguration and Charms, but was unable to remove Fred and George Weasley's magic from Hogwarts, something other professors accomplished with ease.

Few Hogwarts teachers are quite so underestimated as Professor Sprout, the Herbology teacher. A competent witch, she's a specialist in a field that can be very dangerous indeed, and has vast experience of magical plants. Sprout proved her skill during the Battle of Hogwarts, when she turned her knowledge into offensive strategies. Herbology may not sound like a combat arena, but the Death Eaters learned not to count her out.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3465. Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

Way back in October 2024, The Fithian Group, led by former NATO chief John Fithian and founding partner Patrick Corcoran, announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace, one that would help connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners looking to book their movies and effectively cut out the distribution middleman. Today, that vision is now a reality.

The Fithian Group on Wednesday at the American Film Market announced the formal launch of Attend Theatrical Marketplace, the group’s online platform and marketplace for filmmakers and exhibitors that is now live and ready for business.

Attend launches with today just a curated selection of four films, all of whose filmmakers will now be doing the legwork to connect with theaters and find venues at which to exhibit their work. But the platform is already loaded with exhibition partners who will be able to browse available films, with more to be added soon, and Attend will eventually be a fully open platform to any filmmaker who wishes to do outreach directly to theater owners. Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

IndieWire got an early demo of Attend and how it aims to simplify the work that distributors do every day in putting movies into theaters, as well as the work exhibitors have to do in booking movies, paying invoices, and more. And IndieWire will on Wednesday lead a panel discussion at AFM with Corcoran, Charles Beale of the site’s designer Titlepool, and filmmaker Lilian T. Mehrel, whose Tribeca award-winning film “Honeyjoon” will be one of the four inaugural films shopping for theaters.

Beyond “Honeyjoon,” the other three films available on Attend at launch are Kenny Riches’ crime drama “Mouse”; “Spoke,” which is a documentary about firefighters and the trauma they deal with after the fires; and “Censurada,” an LGBTQ+ drama from Marco Garza about forbidden love in 1969 Spain.

The vision of Attend was outlined to IndieWire over a year ago with an indie rom-com called “You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea. The thinking was, if you had a film that could demonstrate it already had an audience and you had a clear sense of where your audience was and how to target them, all you needed were the screens to showcase your movie and the means to get your movie into the hands of those theaters.

That was and remains the tricky part. Few people have the connections with theater owners to be able to reach them and get a film out in any meaningful capacity. This year has produced a number of examples in which enterprising filmmakers have done without distributors and found the audience they already knew was there to release their movies. YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters and made $50 million with his horror movie “Iron Lung.” The documentary “NAZA” skipped a distributor in order to get its story about the IDF out with urgency. Even an AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is next month releasing without the aid of a distributor.

Attend seeks to use technology to simplify that process, to get your film out to an even wider audience and a more targeted one. For filmmakers, the platform is designed to eliminate the guesswork of who you need to talk to, how you reach them, and what attributes a given exhibitor is looking for in a film. For exhibitors, it filters all your titles and screens into one place, and it makes the receiving of deliverables or the payment of invoices more automated than the often tedious work it is for most exhibitors today. It’s exciting to see the whole vision come into fruition.

On the filmmaker end, the way Attend works is you as an individual can upload details and assets about your film, from simple details like its runtime, logline, and genre, to much more granular details about the aspect ratio, the available formats, the awards it has won and festivals it has played, the social networking reach of talent, and many more data points. There may be assets you don’t realize will be significant to a given exhibitor but will jump out as they browse your profile. You can then identify themes that speak to the film’s target audience and narrow the demographics for which your film is intended.

From there, you can filter and browse theaters to identify which theaters would be the best fit for your movie. For instance, Attend has data that can show a theater is within walking distance of a firehouse or that the theater has ties to a local advocacy group that aligns with the themes of the film’s story, and Attend’s predictive AI engine can recommend those theaters that would be available and the best fit for your film. Then, instead of reaching out to each of those theaters individually, filmmakers can easily select all the relevant theaters they want to message and have the option to manually add or subtract more beyond the recommended targets. You can even modify proposed theatrical terms for individual theaters or personalize messages, and as theaters come in, Attend can dynamically estimate P&A spend for those locations.

When theater owners are contacted, they’ll receive push notifications about films that are available for them to review, and they can further browse any available films in the marketplace and do their own outreach. Exhibitors can create tabs and info on any number of their circuit’s screens or locations and can upload in spreadsheets specs like screen size, audio, and seat count that filmmakers can view themselves to better get a sense of which theaters are the best fit. Exhibitors can specify rental prices for individual screens, you can mark your theater as being willing to offer simple four-walling options or that it’s capable of hosting big premieres, whether you want to offer “split screens” or “clean screens,” or you can set terms for how long you’re able to hold a movie. And not only does it also itemize marketing costs, Attend clearly indicates what the share of a film’s box office would be if they were to accept it and program it.

This helps theater owners in a number of ways. It takes the busy work out of things like paying numerous individual vendors or distribution partners, and it lets you download and easily generate a W9 form based on that film’s booking, being able to do so across multiple locations. But for theater owners that generally don’t know what they’re playing until the Monday before, this gives theaters far more advanced leeway and awareness to then be able to do the necessary marketing, put tickets on sale, and actually get butts in seats. All that is especially important for the smaller indies that need that word of mouth.

For now, theaters haven’t linked their loyalty data or other point of sales or scheduling tools to Attend, but that could come with time, and as people actually begin to use the platform, the predictive functionality will improve in the long run.

Corcoran and Fithian see Attend being useful for smaller distributors themselves in the long run, not just individual filmmakers who want to cut out the middleman. Distributors can use it to plan the campaigns of multiple titles and use its automation features to save time and costs. And while today Attend just supports new releases, there’s no reason why older library titles couldn’t be marketed here to exhibitors as well.

Time will tell if filmmakers find Attend an effective form of reaching theaters or if exhibitors adopt the platform widely to make it a useful tool for all parties. But it’s an ambitious vision that if implemented properly could have enormous impacts for the independent film world. And after two years of effort and hype, that day could finally be here.

#3463. Remove your personal info from the web (and stop it coming back)

It seems incredible that anyone can legally create a business which involves scraping your personal data from the web and then selling it, yet here we are. There are literally hundreds of data brokers doing just this.

Personal data bought and sold includes everything from your web-browsing habits and interests to your location history. The least-worst case is that your personal data is purchased by companies wanting to target you with ads. In the worst case, hackers gain access to that data, where it is made available to scammers and identity thieves.

You can fight back using what’s known as “takedown requests.” By law, data brokers have to remove your data if you tell them to. However, this is much easier said than done.

First, you would have to contact literally hundreds of different companies. Second, many of those companies deliberately make takedown links hard to find, then force you to jump through all sorts of hoops in order to issue the requests. Some of them even break the law by not providing the links in the first place.

But even if you succeed, the results won’t last for long. Data brokers are constantly buying new data and adding it to your profile. It’s a constant game of whack-a-mole.

That’s where Incogni comes in. Not only do they do all of the hard work for you across literally hundreds of data brokers, genealogy websites, and social media, but they monitor to ensure that it has been done, scan for the later addition of new data, and issue new takedown requests for that.

Unlike other services, Incogni helps remove your sensitive information from all broker types, including those tricky People Search Sites that are often missed.

With the company’s Unlimited plan, you can even send links you’ve discovered yourself and Incogni will take care of it for you.

#3462. Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

Tom Curley is happy about the election results. Whether they’ll help him get back to work is another matter. The production sound mixer, who won an Oscar for “Whiplash,” told IndieWire he has struggled to find consistent employment since his last gig, “CSI: Vegas,” was canceled in 2024.

He’s picked up some work here and there, but nothing has restored the professional footing Curley said he had just two years ago: a loss that has felt “humiliating.”

“I kind of feel like I was in a car accident almost, and I’m just here staring at the aftermath, wondering how I’m going to pick up the pieces, if I’m ever going to pick up the pieces,” he said. “It’s a very destabilizing thing.” Related Stories Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

Before last week’s midterms, Curley was cautiously optimistic about a proposed federal tax credit designed to keep more film and TV production work inside the U.S. Now, he’s worried the blue wave could inadvertently slow a bill that had been gaining momentum on both sides.

With Republicans meeting such dramatic electoral losses on November 3, Curley fears President Trump could withdraw his support for the proposed tax credit as a kind of punishment.

“All it takes is some hurt feelings to get in the way,” he said.

But the election was mostly good news for Hollywood, right? Democrats won back both chambers of Congress, and Xavier Becerra (also a Democrat) will soon succeed Gavin Newsom as governor of California — still home to the country’s largest film and TV production workforce.

Meanwhile in LA, Nithya Raman beat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after explicitly campaigning to make it easier to shoot here. Raman’s victory was widely seen as a rebuke of the status quo in a city where production jobs have become increasingly difficult to find. It’s also part of a broader Democratic promise to make the economy work better for the people who actually depend on it, crews included.

Yet for the scads of film and TV workers IndieWire spoke to in Los Angeles, being pleased with the election results politically didn’t necessarily mean expecting more work to come their way.

Hollywood is a state of mind, sure. But it’s also a literal place where residents have rent due even when the industry isn’t thriving — and inflation, gig-economy restrictions, SAG-AFTRA contract uncertainty, permitting headaches, artificial intelligence, inaccessible healthcare, corporate consolidation, and, yes, productions increasingly leaving town are making the gaps between paychecks harder to survive.

Legislation can support crews in theory, but film and TV executives still decide what gets made, where it gets made, and who gets hired in the end. For someone like Curley, even one more gig might ease his anxiety and help with the bills. The harder question is what comes after that opportunity wraps, and whether today’s labor market can still offer the people who make movie magic enough for a real living.

The first test for this new establishment comes even before the majority takes office.

In the first quarter of 2025, roughly 46 percent of scripted American projects tracked by Luminate were filmed entirely abroad. That’s part of a broader trend toward international production that has drawn bipartisan concern in the U.S. since the late ‘90s.

Right now, Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Laura Friedman, both Democrats from California, are trying to pass a federal production tax credit through the outgoing Congress during the lame-duck session. The bill was introduced in September with bipartisan backing — including from South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott and Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran, both Republicans returning to Congress next year.

The proposed Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act would lower the cost of hiring film and TV workers in the U.S. by giving eligible productions a national tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying pay. Bonuses could bring that up to 30 percent, although qualifying projects would generally need to cost over $1 million and spend at least 75 percent of their principal photography days in the U.S.

Some domestic post-production and visual effects work would qualify for federal tax breaks, too, and paired with the right state incentives, film producers could reliably use those savings to motivate new work. In fact, Curley said the people who’d hired him before were explicitly waiting for a federal incentive along those lines. That made the proposal feel like a possible job, not just another bill.

“I’ve been in a survival state of mind for the past couple of years, and I would say my nerves are pretty frayed,” he said. “So I’m extra sensitive to potential downfalls to this whole plan that we’re hoping goes through.”

Still, legislators say there’s cause for hope. Rep. Friedman told IndieWire on November 9 that the House bill had 54 cosponsors, evenly split between Democrats and Republicans.

“I’m working to get this done as soon as possible because film and television workers need these jobs back now, not in a few months or a couple of years,” she said.

With weeks left in the current Congress, attaching the credit to a larger bill already headed for a vote might speed things up. But responding to IndieWire, Friedman didn’t identify a specific legislative package that could carry the measure to a scheduled floor date right now. If the proposal doesn’t become law before this session ends, lawmakers will have to reintroduce the initiative next year.

“It will take both parties working together to get this across the finish line, and we are pushing hard to make this much-needed incentive a reality,” Sen. Schiff told IndieWire in a statement.

Friedman noted that, as written, the credit could possibly take effect as early as January 1 — again, if the bill is signed before 2027. That could establish when production could qualify, but it doesn’t tell us when out-of-work crews might actually start getting calls. What’s more, when those job offers finally do come through? They could be far from old creative hubs like Los Angeles.

Richard Sanchez has a production job in California right now, and he knows how much that counts.

“I’m one of the very lucky folks who is working at the moment,” the visual effects editor told IndieWire by email. “But admittedly it’s lean and has been lean for quite a while.”

Tax credits have put states in fierce competition for film and TV jobs, from the first day of shooting to the final edit. And in September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed AB 2319 — specifically creating a separate California tax credit for post-production work. The state is scheduled to start allocating those credits on July 1, 2027, and the yearly budget will ultimately determine how much is available to give out.

“It’s a start, it needs more funding but I hope that brings work in,” Sanchez told IndieWire.

California already makes up to $750 million a year available through its broader film and TV production credit. That previously expanded program began in July 2025 and generally covers 35 percent of qualifying spending, with a higher initial rate for TV series that relocate here. That can help California land a show, but it doesn’t guarantee steady employment for crew members. Studios still decide how many episodes to order and where to send the post-production work.

In the third quarter of 2026, projects in the program accounted for 40.3 percent of scripted on-location filming in Greater Los Angeles (nearly double their share a year earlier), according to FilmLA’s quarterly report. But over the same period, total on-location filming across the region fell 4.8 percent.

“Where the tax credit applies, it’s working to bring productions back to Los Angeles and put local crews to work,” FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches said in a statement to IndieWire. “Still, overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be, and crews and businesses across the region are feeling it.”

FilmLA also counts shoot days, not jobs or paychecks. So, those figures can’t tell us how many people were hired, how much they made, or whether they worked enough to qualify for benefits. One person who responded to IndieWire’s Reddit callout and identified themselves as a Bay Area camera operator said they were working on a union production but doubted they’d log enough hours for health coverage.

Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra called the current program “the floor” during his campaign and pledged to expand. Newsom’s proposal would raise the annual cap to at least $1 billion, make expenses such as actors’ pay eligible, and set aside $100 million a year for indie productions. Those changes still need legislative approval, but Becerra’s first budget will give crews a better idea of what he’s prepared to seek.

As for Curley, he got a brief stint with the U.S. main unit of “Artificial,” which shot partly in San Francisco, but most of the shoot, he said, took place in Italy. A federal credit might make a U.S. production more attractive to filmmakers facing such a choice, but then there’s the question of which state they’ll choose.

Georgia, for example, offers a 20 percent base credit plus another 10 percentage points for productions that promote the state, with no annual cap on how much productions can earn in credits. California and Georgia count different expenses, so the percentages are only part of the calculation.

And a producer weighing L.A. and Atlanta gets to run the numbers both ways — while a crew member who’s spent years building a career in one city has a different calculation to make. If the next show goes across the country, can they afford to follow it? Can they afford to stay put and wait? Either way, more American projects won’t necessarily mean more openings for the crews Hollywood has left behind.

“We can’t always be the cheapest, so we need to be the easiest.” That’s how Pamala Buzick Kim, a co-founder of the production advocacy group Stay in LA, sees the city’s job supporting the industry.

A tax credit can make a shoot look good on paper. But someone still has to get the permits, pay the fees, and figure out what happens when the next location runs across a city line. Buzick Kim said mayor-elect Nithya Raman’s office regularly talked with Stay in L.A. about what was getting in the way of filming and what the city could practically do about it. Those conversations made her optimistic.

“Everybody’s looking after their small piece of the pie, which is what their job is,” Buzick Kim said. “But we have not instituted any infrastructure to look out for our business in Los Angeles as a whole.”

Raman’s office did not immediately respond to IndieWire’s request for comment. But her campaign platform called for a staffed film office within the mayor’s office, clearer permit timelines, lower fees for smaller productions, and regular reviews of neighborhood filming restrictions. She also pledged to work with the county and neighboring jurisdictions so productions could move more easily.

“If we’re going to incentivize more people to roll here we need to cut down permit processing times, lower fees, and lift unnecessary restrictions on local filmmaking,” echoed film and TV editor Andy Young in an email to IndieWire. Young volunteered for Raman in the primary and worked as a paid freelance video editor for her campaign during the general election. (He said he was speaking for himself.)

“I’m excited to have a Mayor that sees LA as an industry town, sees how bleak things are right now, and has a real sense of urgency when it comes to filling sound stages and getting cameras rolling again,” Young wrote.

Some of Raman’s proposed changes will take cooperation across local groups. For example, FilmLA coordinates applications and charges for its services, but city officials approve permits and set some of the fees that FilmLA ultimately collects. A new administration at City Hall will have to work with the people already making those decisions to successfully enact changes.

Of course, for a smaller shoot, every cost makes a difference. FilmLA and the city recently extended their low-impact permit pilot through April 30, 2027, meaning qualifying productions can apply for just $350, compared with the standard $931 application fee. A few days on a commercial can pay the bills between longer jobs, and Buzick Kim wants city residents to see community when film crews take over their block.

“How do we get residents to be more favorable and optimistic about production?” she asked for Stay in LA. “How do we get them understanding that these are your neighbor’s jobs?”

Curley said he didn’t know enough about permitting to say how much a film office would practically help with the issues he’s been facing. After all, for years, the city’s reputation as the best place in the world for movies “was our film office,” he said. Still, taken together, Curley’s dry spell and the Stay in LA pitch assume that literal Hollywood, like anywhere else, must earn its place amongst national competition.

California voters chose new leadership in Washington, the state capital of Sacramento, and LA’s City Hall. But they didn’t get say on who would own two of Hollywood’s biggest studios.

On October 6, less than a month before the election, Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal followed a separate earlier merger in August 2025, when Skydance and Paramount Global combined.

In its November 9 investor update, Skydance said it was aiming for at least $6 billion in annual savings within three years. Those plans include combining back-office functions and using more AI in some corporate workflows.

An August analysis commissioned by L.A. County estimated that the merger could put about 4,500 local film and TV jobs at risk over the next three years. That was an estimate of potential losses, not a count of people already laid off — and it also preceded a fall settlement, which required additional production spending from Skydance. Still, investors got a number and a deadline, while crews are continually being asked to wait and see how much work the combined company will actually have for them.

California and other states did get some promises in writing. A court-approved settlement disclosed in an SEC filing requires Skydance to release a minimum number of films in theaters and bars it from selling or closing the Paramount and Warner Bros. studio lots for five years. The deal also requires the new company to spend at least $1.5 billion more on U.S. filmmaking over that period than the two companies would have spent at their combined pace in 2025. But where will that business go?

Curley, for one, can actually imagine some good coming out of an industry that’s scattered beyond Los Angeles. Maybe more people will get a shot at making something of their own. Maybe there’ll be a burst of indie filmmaking like the one he associates with the ’70s. The Academy Award-winning craftsman can also see doors closing for people who’ve spent their working lives learning how to make movies.

“Maybe this is a good thing for the young people,” he said. “I’m hoping that’s the case anyway.”

For now, Curley already has an Oscar. What he wants is a call time and a chance to create again.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

#3460. iPhone Air 2 is coming next year, here’s why it has more to prove than ever

Next spring, Apple will take the stage to unveil the second-generation iPhone Air to the world, after taking a bit more time to go back to the drawing board and incorporate a second camera into the design. That said, iPhone Air is no longer the flashy cool phone, now iPhone Duo is.

With that being the case, it seems obvious to me that iPhone Air 2 will need to appeal to a wider audience, beyond just the enthusiast crowd.

iPhone Air wasn’t an incredible seller. That said, it was still an incredible marvel of engineering – proving that you can still pack a largely flagship smartphone experience in such a thin design. It wasn’t perfect though, and the compromises alongside its higher price tag meant it only appealed to a small audience.

Now that iPhone Air 2 won’t have the shiny-new-thing factor going for it, it seems almost imperative for Apple to address some of the key shortcomings of the original iPhone Air.

We already know Apple is going to address two of the biggest ones: adding a second camera, as well as a larger battery capacity.

iPhone Air concerns don’t end there, though. There’s also compromised speakers, a compromised connectivity and charging experience, and a compromised camera experience.

iPhone Air has a single mono earpiece speaker. Audio on it isn’t excellent. Luckily, with iPad mini 8, Apple introduced acoustic display – which allows speakers to play through the display glass. Perhaps some of that tech can be taken for iPhone Air 2 to improve the subpar speaker experience.

Another major drawback is connectivity and charging. iPhone Air only supports USB 2, while the Pro iPhones support USB 3. Does this matter to most consumers? Maybe not. When the iPhone Air fetches very close to Pro pricing though, it should offer it. On the charging front of things, iPhone Air only supports 20W MagSafe and 25W fast charging, compared to 25W MagSafe and 60W fast charging on iPhone 18 Pro.

It's nice to wish everything was the best, but the air works great for me. Whatever camera it's got is better than whatever I had 10 years ago, and I'm not a professional photographer, so, it's fine. Battery life and charging speed are better than whatever I had 10 years ago, and I've never had a moment where I regretted either of those issues. I absolutely cannot stand listening to anything on little tiny phone speakers, and I never do, and I never did. I use earbuds all the time. So the speaker is irrelevant to me. What is relevant is, it is thinner and lighter than any phone I've had in 10 years, and THAT I notice every time I pick it up, and every time I slip it in my pocket.

Lastly, the camera. I expect the camera quality to still be limited as a result of smaller sensors, but there are a few things you miss out on with iPhone Air: RAW support, cinematic mode, and macro mode. The latter is more of a result of the phone lacking an ultrawide camera, so ideally we’ll see macro come to iPhone Air 2.

All in all, iPhone Air 2 needs to have a firm position in the lineup. If it’s going to come within $100 of a Pro iPhone, it should offer an experience close to that. The fact that it’s thin should be just another feature, rather than it being a justification for compromise.

#3459. Captain Kirk Hits the Ice as Star Trek Star Officially Joins Netflix’s New Hockey Romance

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Anastasia Allen transferred to Maple Hills to get closer to the Olympics, and Nate Hawkins is trying to make it to the NHL. Both have good reasons to be territorial about practice time, which is exactly what makes their first problem so satisfying. An accident leaves the figure skaters and hockey players with one rink between them, and two people used to getting their way have to agree on who gets the ice.

Netflix has already cast Daisy Jelley (Geek Girl) as Anastasia and Connor Simos (Subversion) as Nate. The latest addition is the person who has to keep the hockey team focused while its captain gets increasingly distracted. For that, Netflix turned to an actor who’s spent the last few years figuring out how to play a young James T. Kirk before he becomes the man everyone expects to take charge.

Netflix has cast Paul Wesley as Coach Neil Faulkner in Icebreaker, its adaptation of Hannah Grace’s bestselling hockey romance. The Vampire Diaries star joins the series as production gets underway in Vancouver, British Columbia. The cast also includes Auliʻi Cravalho as Lola, Gabriel Tierney as Aaron, and Aidan Shaw, who appeared in Heated Rivalry, as Russ. Netflix has yet to announce a premiere date.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

In Grace’s novel, Faulkner is a former NHL player whose career ended after he was hit by a drunk driver, giving his strict approach to coaching some weight with the perfect actor in the role. Nate is still chasing the career Faulkner had, and every practice that turns into a fight over rink time is a practice his team could have spent getting better. Netflix has confirmed Wesley’s role, with the specifics of Faulkner’s story on screen still to come.

Icebreaker also comes with an audience that has had years to decide what it wants to see from Maple Hills. The novel spent 70 consecutive weeks on the New York Times bestseller list and has sold nearly 5 million copies worldwide, according to data supplied by Netflix. Readers will recognize a couple of names in the supporting cast that could matter well beyond Nate and Anastasia’s story. Russ and Henry, played by Shaw and Devin Craig, go on to lead their own Maple Hills books, Wildfire and Daydream, respectively. The series in production adapts the first book, with Gossip Girl alum Amanda Lasher as showrunner and Jade Halley Bartlett as creator.

Icebreaker does not currently have a release date. Stay tuned with Collider for updates on all of your favorite romances, both on the ice and off!

#3458. Alexander Skarsgård’s Beloved Fantasy Horror Adaptation Is Officially Leaving Hulu After 4 Years

Alexander Skarsgård's hit horror fantasy TV show has been available on Hulu since January 2023, but if you haven't watched it yet, now's the time before it leaves the service. In the age of streaming, with shows at our fingertips, it feels like we have all the time in the world to watch what we want.

Gone are the days of waiting up to make sure we catch the latest episode of Lost, or lamenting the fact that we had some obligation the night of a season premiere. Now, when we want to watch a show, we can just watch it, at our own pace, and on our own time. Unfortunately, that's not always the case.

Shows and movies are not guaranteed to stay on one streaming platform, even if they've been there for years. Take True Blood, HBO's horror-fantasy series that landed on Hulu in early 2023 but is now set to leave at the end of the year. Hulu users may have thought they could watch the show whenever, but now they only have a few weeks.

True Blood premiered in 2008 on HBO, based on Charlaine Harris' The Southern Vampire Mysteries series. The series is set in a world where vampires are a known section of the population, and whose murderous impulses are kept in check by synthetic blood known as "Tru Blood".

The series involves vampires' attempts to assimilate into wider society, and the introduction of other creatures from fantasy and myth, including werewolves, fairies, witches, and more. A massive hit for the first few seasons, it started to fall off toward the end, which is why it's not always ranked among HBO's best originals.

Still, True Blood was one of the first major fantasy TV shows intended for mature audiences. Game of Thrones is usually considered the major turning point in fantasy television, proving that major budgets and mature storylines could find huge audiences, but HBO may not have had the same confidence in Game of Thrones as it did without the success of True Blood.

True Blood first came to Hulu in January 2023, but some sources say that the series will be leaving the platform on December 31, 2026 (via Instagram). All seven seasons and 80 episodes are available on the service, and with each episode being 45–64 minutes long, you'll probably want to start binge-watching now if you intend to finish.

Warner Bros. Discovery did begin licensing out HBO original shows once that merger happened, and with the recent Skydance acquisition, it's possible the title could be licensed out again. Though True Blood will be coming off Hulu, the new owners of HBO could be interested in making a similar deal soon.

Even if True Blood is coming off Hulu, it will still be available to stream on HBO Max through 2027, as would be expected of an HBO Original. However, there are a few cases of HBO Originals no longer being available on the service. That's what happened with Raised by Wolves and Mrs. Fletcher.

There's no guarantee that True Blood will always be made available for streaming, another case to be made for the value of physical media, so if you have any interest in the show, you had better try to catch it sooner rather than later.

#3457. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

“Godzilla Minus Zero” almost pulled of a Godzilla-times-three on its opening weekend, earning $31.6 million in North America to nearly triple the domestic debut of its 2023 predecessor “Godzilla Minus One.” With that Godzilla math, it destroyed the record for the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film.

It was a crowning moment for the speciality distributor GKIDS. Founded in 2008, the label primarily built itself as a distributor of foreign language animated features, most notably with its acquisition of the North American distribution rights to the Studio Ghibli library. As a day-one employee of GKIDS, and its president since 2017, Dave Jesteadt has helped expand the stateside audience for subtitled features. After a 2025 acquisition by Toho, the Japanese film industry giant behind “Godzilla,” the reach of GKIDS is wider than ever with “Minus Zero,” which drew a box office debut that some studio tentpoles this year would envy. Related Stories Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work? Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

“Anecdotally, so many people I know are like, ‘I took my dad this movie and he doesn’t go to any subtitle movies,'” Jesteadt told IndieWire. “Godzilla brings us together. If we’re spreading the gospel of foreign cinema, and Godzilla is a vehicle to get people to engage with great films and deep themes, then I’m all for it.”

After a flashy premiere at the New York Film Festival and a historic cume from IMAX and other premium large-format auditoriums, Jesteadt digs into how GKIDS helped “Minus Zero” come to America.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: “Godzilla Minus One” was seen as a breakout success in 2023, with $57 million in North America. What lessons did GKIDS take away from Toho‘s release of “Minus One” in building toward this big opening for “Minus Zero”?

Dave Jesteadt: GKIDS joined the Toho Group in October 2024, but our story of working together on this began before that, back in 2023. GKIDS had “The Boy and the Heron” from Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli in theaters just a week after “Godzilla Minus One” opened, which was being handled by Toho’s L.A. office at the time. We got to know that team because we had these two films in theaters, sort of competing for similar audience profiles.

In terms of lessons that both sides took, it’s that you can really drive conversation with theaters as a source of celebration and community. When we joined the Toho Group, we took in the team that worked on “Minus One.” We re-released “Shin Godzilla” in 2025 as a test for bringing modern Japanese “Godzilla” films to theaters. Then the planning for “Minus Zero” really began in terms of how we could build and improve on the audience that “Minus One” already found.

Did “Minus Zero” get a bigger marketing spend stateside? How did you consider which people to reach to expand the audience for a Japanese “Godzilla” film?

I can’t give a specific number, but I’d say that we’re very efficient and very mindful of how we can reach the audience in the most direct way possible. For this film, we have the great benefit of our colleagues at Toho International owning and operating Godzilla.com, overseeing merchandise licensing. They have direct communication with the “Godzilla” fan as they exist in America.

But the other goal is to reach, as “Minus One” did, an audience that hadn’t engaged in Japanese “Godzilla” films. We also balanced reaching that core “Godzilla” fan and making sure that they turn out with this desire to continue the story from “Minus One,” reminding people that these films from director Takashi Yamazaki really speak to broader feelings today. They have prestigious bona fides through playing film festivals and great critical reviews. We’re leading with the quality of the film, making people feel that this is a very safe choice — not just if you like spectacle, but that this is going to be one of the best films of the year.

The New York Film Festival premiere played as a flex, especially after a stretch where Hollywood would premiere summer blockbusters at Cannes, draw mediocre reviews, and then have to weather weeks of bad buzz for their expensive tentpoles. With the NYFF premiere, “Minus Zero” was positioned as a prestige object. Is that the aura you were trying to cultivate around it?

I think so. Godzilla has been one of the most famous characters in the world. There’s a big audience that you can potentially address. But the “Minus” franchise takes it into more realistic, human-centered stories. That differentiates it. It is a risk to go to a film festival; I think that has been pretty well-argued. It is a risk anytime you want to share something with the world early before you open, especially when you have such high hopes about how it’s going to go. On the other hand, this was a really important way to demonstrate confidence.

“Minus Zero” opened in more than 3,200 theaters, roughly 1,000 more theaters than “Minus One.” How much did you expand its presence in premium large-format auditoriums?

“Minus Zero” was the first Japanese production filmed for IMAX. That was a central part of the very first announcement and it was a defining part of the marketing campaign. IMAX mentioned it was the highest-indexed opening gross on IMAX screens for an opening weekend in the U.S. We had Godzilla Day on November 3, with IMAX early access screenings globally. So, PLFs definitely played a big presence: Imax, 4DX, Dbox, and others. That’s very unusual for a subtitled foreign film.

It speaks to the expectations for high quality that audiences brought. The PLF story is a way to reinforce production quality. Everyone is saying, “You have to see it in the biggest screen possible with the best sound.” I’ve seen many, many beautiful foreign films. They often end up playing circuits to audiences that are very passionate, but don’t have access to those kind of screens. So it’s a privilege to be able to play a film on the kind of screen that’s typically reserved for the biggest mainstream titles.

How long are you staying in IMAX and PLFs?

It depends on the market. We’re definitely here for the rest of this week. But as “The Odyssey” and other titles have demonstrated, there’s such draw to these moments. It can even create this quest to see something in multiple formats. But as we head into the Thanksgiving frame, the Hollywood competition is obviously huge. We’re realistic about that, even while we’re trying to encourage people to see it as soon and as often as they can.

The reported statistic that more than 70 percent of grosses came from PLFs seems a bit of a double-edged sword to me. It speaks to a high regard for the film among consumers, but it also might indicate that it has a specialized audience that may only want to see the movie in a premium format. Is that a consideration GKIDS takes in, particularly when other titles are taking those auditoriums in the coming weeks?

Obviously, PLFs are time-sensitive. It’s not just about performance, but also about new titles coming in. We’re up against the biggest studios in the world. I’m obviously thrilled that we were able to get so many and I’m thrilled that people saw it that way. I also encourage everyone to just see it in regular theaters too. The way that it was mastered and the way that director Yamazaki made the film is so you won’t have a bad experience in any house watching it. But with any of these core fandoms, there’s a lot of interest in seeing something “the right way.” I’m happy for that, but then the hope is they tell their friends and we continue the growth from there.

You’ve been with GKIDS since its inception and have played a major part in growing the American audience for foreign language cinema. What do you think has changed in the marketplace that has allowed a Japanese “Godzilla” film to now find a much broader audience in the West than it could find before?

There’s no doubt that the quality of the films really helps. “Minus One” was a fantastic film. It won the Oscar for visual effects and became an audience darling. But really, the thing that’s changed the most is that younger generations are much more open to subtitled and foreign cinema than they would have been 10 or 20 years ago. We’ve entered an age of opportunity where what can constitute a hit film is really broadening. That gives me a lot of optimism compared to negative stories about the overall economics of the industry. GKIDS has been bringing subtitled animated movies and anime to audiences for almost 20 years and seeing that audience grow naturally. At first, dubs were essential; now, they’re not.

Though GKIDS isn’t producing these films, I’m curious if, as a distributor, you think that Japanese productions like “Minus Zero” are now being developed and produced with more of a global audience in mind.

The films are still intrinsically Japanese and are basically impossible to separate from the cultural tradition of “Godzilla” in Japan, as well as the overall Japanese film industry. On the other hand, there’s no doubt that the property has the ability to reach a global audience. The popularity with the “Minus” series is really a focus on quality, and how its storytelling is rooted in a time and a place that feels authentically Japanese. Although it deals with a post-war moment in Japanese history, it is incredibly contemporary in terms of the thoughts and preoccupations of a global audience.

So I don’t think there’s necessarily a change in focus. I would say that the audience and the director are in a much more direct conversation. On social media now, everything is auto-translated. You can see real-time active conversation between Japanese fans and viewers commenting about the film with American or Spanish or European audience. Everyone is able to share their thoughts or opinions about some of these themes in a way that brings local perspective to the table. By creating something that feel like it’s created for a specific audience, ironically, you end up making it feel more universal, just because it feels more lived in.

Do you think we are headed to a world where a Japanese “Godzilla” film can outgross a Western “Godzilla” film in North America?

I don’t really think about that. I’m very competitive against a lot of people, but the “Godzilla” franchise has benefited from having a lot of flavors to it. By building that big tent, it ends up being a character that has endured.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now in theaters.

If you are looking for something a little more rugged, the UAG Mouve case is worth looking into. UAG has always focused on protective cases, and this one brings the same philosophy and design language while adding an adjustable built-in kickstand. You get:

#3455. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

Anker’s new MagGo Pro 2 power bank offers active cooling, 25W MagSafe fast charging, 10,000mAh of capacity, and a smart display – all in one package. Anker touts it as the fastest and coolest wireless power bank on the market.

Thanks to the active cooling within this power bank, you’ll notice it doesn’t get as hot as other power banks on the market. This also helps it charge faster, since it doesn’t have to throttle as quickly to keep the temperature manageable.

As a result, you can charge an iPhone 17 Pro up to 50% in just 25 minutes with this battery bank. It also supports up to 45W of output via USB-C.

On the side of the power bank, you’ll notice a smart display. This display can show you the battery level, how quickly its charging an attached device (either wirelessly or with USB-C), the internal temperature of the battery bank, as well as the battery health. You can rotate between all of these options by pressing the power button.

This power bank also offers a kickstand, which I’ve found to be one of my favorite features on recent MagSafe battery banks. It makes it easy to just prop up your phone and watch a video, no matter the environment.

If you have an iPhone Duo, this power bank will extend past the bottom of the phone. If you rotate it and use the kickstand, there’s no issue propping up your phone and charging it.

Lastly, the MagGo Pro 2 comes in a bunch of fun colors, including a burgundy to match the new iPhone 18 Pro. It’s also available in silver, blue, and gray.

If the Anker MagGo Pro 2 Power Bank interests you, you can pick one up for $109.99 on Amazon.
