#3452. Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before

Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film, German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “Everytime” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie.”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel, either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.

#3451. Guy Ritchie’s Fantasy Epic That Bombed at the Box Office Finds Streaming Success

Guy Ritchie has been on a hot streak in recent years, despite some box-office underperformers. Earlier this year, In The Grey, starring Henry Cavill and Jake Gyllenhaal, came out in theaters but found true success on streaming. Meaning, his real audience is watching at home, making each project an instant hit with brilliant viewership records. He then focused on the silver screen, directing several episodes of Tom Hardy’s gangster drama, MobLand, and making series like Young Sherlock, starring Hero Fiennes Tiffin as a 19-year-old Sherlock, that has emerged as a fan favorite.

As Ritchie’s impressive resume grows, fans are returning to some of his best movies like John Krasinski’s Fountain of Youth or the Robert Downey Jr.-starring Sherlock Holmes. Among such titles is also Charlie Hunnam-led King Arthur: The Legend of the Sword. Ritchie took the Arthurian legend and gave it his own fast-paced, witty, and gritty action touch. Initially envisioned as a multi-movie franchise, the action-adventure flick failed to impress its audience at the time.

Hunnam plays Arthur as a reluctant hero, a cheeky man who doesn’t want to come face to face with his past and has to conquer internal trauma before winning the rebellion. He garnered a lot of praise for his intense physical commitment and raw charisma. However, it couldn’t save the feature; it earned $148.7 million worldwide on a $175 million budget. While critics gave it a 31% Rotten Tomatoes rating, audiences were more generous, giving it a 69% rating. And now the audiences’ love is catapulting the feature to new heights. King Arthur: Legend of the Sword has climbed Netflix's top 10 charts, as per FlixPatrol. The feature stands tall at the sixth spot among films like A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, The Day After Tomorrow, The Croods, The Mummy, 10000 BC, and more.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

We follow Arthur, who was raised in the back alleys of the city after his father died and his birthright was stolen. He grows up on the rough city streets, learning to fight and fend for himself as a skilled fighter alongside a close-knit street gang. Years later, when the legendary sword Excalibur reemerges, Arthur embraces his destiny after pulling the sword from the stone and leads a rebellion against his tyrannical uncle, Vortigern. The filmmakers strip the legend of its noble culture and chivalry, replacing it with themes rooted in street smarts and psychological survival.

#3450. Indie App Spotlight: ‘CueFlip’ automatically turns the page for your sheet music

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

If you find yourself playing an instrument with sheet music, flipping the page often requires you to stop playing to turn the page. CueFlip solves that. You can teach it how you play a song, then it can turn the page for you whilst listening.

CueFlip doesn’t just assume how it should turn the page, you can explicitly teach it how to. That starts with either a live rehearsal, or a recording you can share with it. Then, you mark the turns.

CueFlip also has a built in dictionary, where you can see certain notes on a page so you can learn how the composer meant to play them, rather than needing to guess them. Many times, these terms will be in other languages, but CueFlip offers built in translation with up to 13 languages. CueFlip covers over 20,000 terms, and it can pull terms from scanned scores as well.

Lastly, CueFlip has a neat little feature with Face ID. If you wink with your right eye, you can manually turn a page forward, and if you wink with your left eye, it’ll go backwards. Similarly, CueFlip also works with manual Bluetooth page turners in addition to the automatic turning, in case you need it.

Here’s why 15 year old classical guitarist Yuze Pan from Beijing decided to build CueFlip:

I play in the Primal Guitar Quartet, and page turns kept breaking up our rehearsals. Paper means taking a hand off the strings, a pedal or a wink is one more thing to remember in the middle of a phrase, and timed turns can’t follow a performer who speeds up and slows down. My first attempt, in 2025, didn’t work. In May 2026 I started again, this time by reading the research on audio alignment, and brought every new build to the quartet’s daily rehearsals.

CueFlip is available for free on the App Store for iPhone and iPad users running iOS and iPadOS 16.4 and later. The free version includes PDFs with annotations and automatic page turning for one score, whereas Pro unlocks unlimited page turning, the music dictionary, wink to turn pages, and much more for $4.99/month and $29.99/year.

#3449. Scarlet Witch's Avengers: Doomsday Return Confirms An MCU First

Warning: This post contains spoilers for VisionQuestScarlet Witch is officially back in the Marvel Cinematic Universe for Avengers: Doomsday, and Elizabeth Olsen's return as Wanda Maximoff confirms a long-awaited first. The powerful witch became one of the MCU's most popular characters throughout the Infinity Saga and WandaVision. That's why it came as such a devastating blow to many when Scarlet Witch died in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

Given the magical aspect of her abilities, theories have persisted for years that Wanda would be back, despite being crushed by Wundagore. Marvel finally confirmed this hope was not misplaced, as VisionQuest episode 8's post-credits scene confirmed she is alive. This came as Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) was shown lifting the rubble and reviving Scarlet Witch, wanting her power for himself.

The scene and Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday countdown clock were used to confirm Wanda's return just over one month before the blockbuster hits theaters on December 18. She will be involved in another multiverse-threatening event, and seemingly sliding into a villain role once again under Doom's influence.

As exciting as it is to have Scarlet Witch back in any capacity, the nature of her role in Avengers: Doomsday is a bigger deal than many may realize at first. Her presence gives more insight into Doom's plan. In a first for the MCU, the Avengers are going to encounter a true supervillain team.

Throughout the MCU, the Avengers have encountered some formidable villains. Loki, Ultron, and Thanos each made saving the world a difficult task for Earth's Mightiest Heroes. But in each case, they primarily operated alone and without the aid of additional superpowers. Thanos is the arguable exception here, as he had Ebony Maw's telekinesis to aid him a few times. Each of them instead relied on having massive armies to support their plans.

Previously, it was assumed that Doom would follow a similar path. After all, Victor von Doom is known for creating Doombots in the comics, so he could very easily have an entire legion of robots at his command to fight the Avengers when the time comes in Doomsday. Scarlet Witch's confirmed return and recruitment by the Latverian ruler shows he's taking a different approach.

This is now the second time Marvel Studios has shown Doom collecting a powerful MCU hero ahead of Doomsday. The first instance came in Avengers Endgame: Encore's new scenes, which revealed Doom has also taken Hulk. Those two scenes confirm that a key part of Doom's plan to conquer the multiverse is getting some of Earth-616's most powerful characters to fight for him.

Doom, Hulk, and Scarlet Witch are officially the MCU's first supervillain team, then. The franchise has never united multiple "villains" like this before, and the Avengers have never had to fight a group of opponents with their combined strength. This becomes an exciting way for Avengers: Doomsday to still feel fresh.

One of the seemingly unavoidable clichés of the Avengers movies previously is that each main villain needed an expendable army of cannon fodder so the films could achieve the level of action desired. The Avengers would have ended a lot faster if Loki didn't have the Chitauri army to fight the original Avengers. The same is true for Avengers: Age of Ultron, as Ultron would've been defeated even faster if not for the Ultron Sentries. Thanos wouldn't have been able to acquire the Infinity Stones as easily if not for the Black Order and The Outriders on his side.

Doombots may still be in Avengers: Doomsday and prove to be Doom's solution to needing enough enemies for the Avengers, Thunderbolts, X-Men, and Fantastic Four to fight at once. However, Hulk and Scarlet Witch being on his side means that there will be some additional powerful characters that the heroes have to focus on defeating. Wanda and Hulk could take on most of the heroes by themselves, so they, paired with Doom, give the Avengers an incredibly difficult task.

This should ensure that Avengers: Doomsday's third act battle goes beyond senseless action. There should be real stakes at play as the heroes are forced to confront old friends, which could go beyond just Hulk and Scarlet Witch. Even if Doom holds no personal connection to Iron Man for the heroes to struggle with, they will be in a tough spot as they have to fight their former teammates to try and stop Doom's plan.

Doom, Scarlet Witch, and Hulk are about as powerful a trio as you can form in the MCU, but it would be a surprise if this was the end of the supervillain team. Victor is clearly going after people who are incredibly strong and who could disappear from the MCU timeline without anyone really noticing.

It seems inevitable that Doctor Strange will expand Doom's team to a quartet. He was last seen entering the Dark Dimension to stop an incursion with Clea. Strange is one of the only sorcerers with the power to potentially stand up to Doom, so it would make a ton of sense for Victor to pull him onto his side. He might not even have to force Stephen to do this, as the former surgeon has shown he's willing to make controversial decisions and sacrifice others if it keeps more people safe.

We also know that Doom has three Latverian witches on his side in Doomsday. One of these is surely Scarlet Witch. One is presumed to be Sandra Hüller's mystery character. The other could be anyone from Clea to Sylvie to Agatha to a revived Ancient One, assuming they are true "witches" and have some form of magical powers.

Doom's team could also be how some of Doomsday's other biggest missing MCU characters enter the equation. He may have taken Captain Marvel to keep her power from stopping him. Spider-Man could have even been a target. His search for powerful teammates could have even taken him to other universes, with Halle Berry's Storm or Famke Janssen's Jean Grey other formidable heroes he may not want to face.

In any case, Avengers: Doomsday's finale has become a whole lot more interesting now. Seeing the Avengers, Thunderbolts, X-Men, and Fantastic Four have to fight Doctor Doom, Scarlet Witch, Hulk, and possibly more secret team members is an exciting prospect that could deliver one of the biggest and craziest third acts in MCU history.

#3448. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on DeWalt, Milwaukee, and Ryobi Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. #3447. Chromagraph Camera is exactly the camera app I’ve been looking for on iPhone

Last week, movie director Rian Johnson announced a surprise new camera app for iPhone that reimagines what a smartphone photo should look like. Many people would agree that Apple’s iPhone photos are a tad bit overprocessed.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo introduced a new film texture option, but in my view, it’s a bit too exaggerated. Chromagraph Camera, on the other hand, feels pretty perfect.

Attempts have been made to improve iPhone photos for years, but they all feel a little bit too heavy, in my view. Most camera apps for iPhone require you to dial settings in. While that can be appropriate for certain settings, I ultimately want my iPhone to just be a point and shoot experience. If I wanted the perfect photo, I’d be using my camera.

That said, iPhone photos just don’t look super excellent out of the box. It’s not a limitation of hardware. If you take a RAW iPhone photo and edit it yourself, you can actually get surprisingly good results. Apple’s camera app just has poor defaults.

When Apple introduced the film grain feature on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, I was actually quite interested in it. It was certainly my favorite camera feature of the phone when I briefly tried out the iPhone 18 Pro. For some reason though, the film look just feels a bit exaggerated on iPhone Duo.

Apps like Adobe’s Project Indigo have gotten really close in terms of look, but the fact that there’s so much time spent post-processing means it’s often inconvenient. I’ve also had a few instances of losing photos because the app closed in the background while it was still processing the photo.

User reviews tell a different story. No trial option is a non- starter for me.

When Chromagraph Camera was announced, I was quite interested. I paid the $12.99, and I’ve been happy with the results. I tweeted some of my sample photos when I just got the app, and it’s been well worth it.

$12.99 may be a higher starting price, but if you really want an iPhone camera app that just takes good looking photos without a lot of hassle, it works really well.

#3445. Apple aiming to make Siri ‘more like an agent’ as soon as next year: report

Apple finally shipped its long awaited personalized Siri with iOS 27. The company lived up to its promises, and delivered on its hefty goals that it set out back in 2024.

That said, Siri still lacks in terms of proactively taking actions for you, a feature that many AI companies are actively working towards. Apple might come around on that next year, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The company is also experimenting with a new engineering pipeline that might make faster development possible.

In recent months, companies like Meta and SpaceXSI have gone all-in on new agentic AI interfaces that can carry out tasks for you. Muse and Grok Bot are agents that have their own virtual machines and can proactively handle tasks in the background for you, then deliver results.

Apple has a lot of potential to deliver in this space, especially given all of the frameworks they’ve built up over the years, like App Intents. With Apple, you hypothetically wouldn’t need to depend on as much computer-use ability, making certain tasks a lot less expensive.

According to Mark Gurman in his Power On newsletter, Apple could debut its own proactive version of Siri as soon as next year:

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

It remains to be seen what Apple will ultimately ship here, but with the right execution, Apple certainly has high potential to compete in this space.

A major part of better execution is having a better process. According to Gurman, Apple is also giving engineers more time to code and explore, rather than spend as much time integrating features within the operating system.

Typically, each of these stages is four weeks. With the first cycle of iOS 28 development, Apple is allotting 6 weeks to coding and 2 weeks to integration. This change was likely driven by the massive advances in agentic coding tools in the past couple years:

For this cycle, though, Apple has done things differently for the M1 milestone. Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence. Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in.

#3444. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3443. Why Scarlett Johansson's Newest Role Proved To Be One Of Her Most Challenging Yet

EXCLUSIVE: The newest Scarlett Johansson movie presented new challenges for the prolific star.

Johansson is a two-time Academy Award nominee, having been recognized for her performances in Jojo Rabbit and Marriage Story. Along with these accolades, she has the second-highest box office of all time for any actor at $15.6 billion, with the many Marvel Cinematic Universe movies featuring her as Black Widow/Natasha Romanoff being key contributors to that total, in addition to 2016's Jungle Book, Jurassic World Rebirth, Sing, and Sing 2.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Tatiana Hullender for Ray Gunn, Johansson was asked about the experience of voicing pop star Venus Nova, who has many different sides to her, in the new animated movie. The Marriage Story star explained that one of the challenges was that there were sometimes months between voice recording sessions, making it difficult to pick up where she left off while playing the complex character created by director and writer Brad Bird. Check out Johansson and Bird's comments below:

Scarlett Johansson: It's a bit of a journey because when you're doing voice recording, it's over a long period of time. It could be months, actually, before I hear from Brad that he needs me again. And when you come back to it, you may have a different perspective on it, or he may have a new perspective on some version of it because he's trying out stuff, like, "Actually, this is better when it's more playful. We had done it in a more sarcastic way, but it's reading as mean, so let's try this." You get a long time to live in it, and you get better at it too.

The character is very complex, and there's so much to her. We find her in a moment of deep personal crisis. That's when we're introduced to her, and she goes on this very moving journey of self-discovery throughout the film, and self-realization. One thing I will say is challenging about coming back to it is that you have to remember, "Where was I?" I would sometimes ask, "Can you play me what I recorded before?" You have to remember where your voice was at.

Brad Bird: Because it's different sides of the character, and the different sides sound different.

Since Venus is a pop star, Johansson not only had to voice the many different sides of the character, but also sing them too. She was asked whether this was different or more challenging from her previous musical experience, which include the movies Sing, Sing 2, and The Jungle Book.

Scarlett Johansson: It was hard. We had a finite amount of time to do it, and we had a lot of work to do. When we meet her, the character starts out churning out these bubblegum, earworm pop and dance hits, and it very much felt like she was just servicing the audience.

Brad Bird: And yet you can't stop thinking about them!

Scarlett Johansson: Yeah, they were stuck in my head forever! But then she's singing a real confession of her true feelings and her desires, and she's finally singing from her truest self. I luckily had Kimbra there to help me find all of that stuff, because she's obviously a brilliant musical mind, and a very sensitive artist, so she understood all of that. Actually, this character is a collaboration of us; we were working on it together, and her own empathy for the character's situation is all baked into it.

Ray Gunn takes place in an alternate future, in the city of Metropia, where Venus is implicated in a murder, with the accusation threatening to destroy her career. Sam Rockwell voices the titular character, a private investigator hired by Venus' husband, Arnold (Bobby Cannavale), to spy on her, which becomes more complicated as he develops romantic feelings for the pop star. Other key characters are Ray's alien detective partner, Eye-ra (Tom Waits), and alien mob boss Francis "Slugsy" Xavier (Matt Berry).

While Bird is best known for directing and writing Pixar movies like The Incredibles, Ratatouille, and Incredibles 2, he has had the idea for Ray Gunn since the 1990s, and it was inspired by noir films such as The Maltese Falcon, Chinatown, and The Big Lebowski.

The movie was produced by Skydance Animation and will be distributed by Netflix, beginning with a limited theatrical release (including on 70mm screens) on December 4 before coming to the streaming platform on December 18. Bird directed the new film, developed the story, co-wrote the screenplay with Matthew Robbins, and was one of the producers.

#3442. Report: John Ternus pushing Craig Federighi to speed up Apple software engineering

In the past few years, a major Apple story (especially in the age of AI) has been that the company isn’t moving fast enough in the space to keep up with competitors. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, new Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly pushing on software chief Craig Federighi to ‘accelerate’ Apple’s roadmap for software.

At the moment, there’s no indication that Apple’s well known software SVP Craig Federighi will be leaving the company. In fact, Craig has made it a very low priority of his to develop a succession plan in any sense, per Mark Gurman. That said, Ternus still wants to see change in how Craig Federighi thinks about Apple’s software strategy:

In recent weeks, Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, who became Apple’s AI czar following last year’s dismissal of its former AI leader. Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri.

A large part of Federighi’s approach has been how hands-on he is, resulting in his viewpoint shaping how Apple’s software development goes to a large extent. That’s left team members feeling that they have ‘limited influence’ over what happens:

Federighi is known for taking an especially hands-on role in meetings and major decisions, with some employees describing a management style that can leave little room for competing ideas to gain traction. He is also known for vigorously debating opposing viewpoints, using his command of technical details and ability to argue his position to push back against proposals he disagrees with. That approach has at times frustrated members of the software engineering and design teams, some of whom believe they have limited influence over the direction of products.

Another part is that Federighi reportedly only plans for a 12-18 month timeframe, versus the years-long roadmaps used in hardware engineering. These are some of the gaps that Apple may want to bridge in the coming years.

Separately, Vision Pro and Siri AI leader Mike Rockwell is still seriously considering stepping down. He’s currently vice president of Siri engineering:

The management concerns go beyond Federighi. Mike Rockwell, who created the Vision Pro headset in addition to leading the development of Siri AI, continues to seriously consider stepping down. That could mean leaving his role as vice president of Siri engineering — or Apple altogether — next year. Such a move would be a major blow, given his role in bringing the new Siri to market after an embarrassing two-year delay.

Interesting timing on this article. I’m sitting here with two laptops: one running Tahoe and the other one running Golden Gate, both of them full of bugs and issues that should’ve never been released outside of Apple, and thinking how great Apple’s hardware is, but how terrible their software has become. I don’t know the inner workings of Apple, so I’ve never wanted to outright blame Federighi, but given that he’s at the top of the software ladder, I can only think that he’s most likely the problem. For all I know he could be holding it altogether, but then I read something like this and makes me think that it might be time for him to go.

I don’t know about accelerating their software, I feel like their software has felt rushed and unfinished for the last 10 years or so, and increasingly so each year, but I think what the article really means is speed up the advancement in the AI aspect of Apple’s software, not actually rushing out their software in general.

In the same report, Gurman also reported that Apple is experimenting with a new development pipeline, giving engineers 50% more time to code and explore more, and spend less time on integration, as coding agents have improved.

It remains to be seen what else might change at Apple to enable faster development timelines, though it seems likely that Craig Federighi may have to release his ‘firm grip’ on the software engineering org, and instead allow some other leaders to blossom and act on their own accord.

As his famous, genre-breaking cowboy Woody, Hanks returned alongside Buzz (Tim Allen), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and the rest of the gang in Toy Story 5. After a mixed response to the fourth installment, Toy Story 5 was a return to form for Pixar's most important franchise.

Collider's Taylor Gates gave the movie an 8/10 rating in her review, saying, "The impressive fifth installment not only justifies its existence but feels like a necessary response to how much the world has changed in the past three decades." This was one of several near-perfect responses to the film, which no doubt helped it on its way past the $1 billion barrier at the global box office, currently ranking as the year's third-highest-grossing film. As Hanks fans bask in the glory of a successful return to form for the actor, they will rejoice further, as it has been confirmed that one of his most endearing movies is being given the reboot treatment.

Officially, Hanks' 1998 rom-com favorite, You've Got Mail, is being rebooted at Warner Bros. Jason Orley is attached to direct, 17 years after he was Nancy Meyers' assistant whilst working on the film It's Complicated. Orley is also reportedly working on a script that is based on a previous take by Deborah Kaplan and Harry Elfont, with Neal Moritz and Tania Landau set to produce under the Original Film banner. Sadly, this is about all we know so far, with plot details being kept tightly under wraps.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

After successfully teaming up on 1993's Sleepless in Seattle, director Nora Ephron and stars Hanks and Meg Ryan reunited for 1998's You've Got Mail to even greater box office success. Against a reported production budget of $65 million, the film returned more than $250 million worldwide, split between a domestic haul of $115 million and a further $135 million from overseas markets. The film came out during a golden period for Hanks, released in the same year as his critical darling Saving Private Ryan and just a year before the beloved Toy Story 2 and The Green Mile.

#3439. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3438. macOS 27.3 could change how you grant AI agents Full Disk Access, here’s how

In its blog post, Apple announced that apps will require “very explicit user action” to have Full Disk Access on your Mac. At the time of the announcement, Apple didn’t make it super clear what that would actually mean. Now, we have an idea of what’s to come.

Code sifter pdfu posted on X that Apple will be getting rid of a clever loophole that developers could use to make it easier for users to enable Full Disk Access. In current versions of macOS, if an app requests a file that would require Full Disk Access, the system denies the request and logs the app as an option in the Settings app for enabling Full Disk Access.

At that point, developers often prompt users to open that section of the Settings app and flip the toggle.

Starting as soon as macOS 27.3, apps that request files outside of the permission scope will no longer get logged, and as a result, won’t show up as an option for quickly toggling Full Disk Access, per leaker pdfu.

macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that… https://t.co/zjUuEh7EIb

At the moment, developers can still request users to drag an app icon to the Settings panel to enable Full Disk Access, even once the feature flag for the aforementioned change is enabled. To me, it still doesn’t quite feel like you’ll need “very explicit user action” to enable Full Disk Access, but it’s possible this will change in the future. This is all still in development.

All in all, I’m not fully convinced that this solves the core problem. Developers are requesting Full Disk Access because they’d like to tap into things like iMessage, and there hasn’t been a better way of doing so. As long as that demand is there, users will likely still have to enable Full Disk Access and risk all sorts of other data, just so they can share their texts with an agent.

Granted, pdfu also mentions the idea of Private Folders, which could potentially allow users to grant scoped access to just the iMessage database folder. It’s unclear if that’ll be possible since there’s little detail on how Private Folders will work. If that’s the case, then hopefully Full Disk Access can stop being the default permission you have to provide for any personal data.

#3434. Disney's $823M Fantasy Epic With A Sequel On The Way Crosses Massive Streaming Milestone

Disney's fantasy epic that made $823 million at the box office and has a sequel in development has officially crossed a massive streaming milestone. Disney's fantasy movies are often relegated to the world of animation, with plenty of high-profile stories that have made massive amounts of money at the box office. This includes both Frozen movies, the Moana films, and 2021's Encanto, which each have very different approaches to their respective worlds. But there's also Pixar, which reigns supreme with some of its massively successful fantasy films.

One of its biggest success stories over the last decade has been Coco. The 2017 animated musical fantasy movie follows a 12-year-old boy named Miguel in Mexico, who accidentally finds himself in the Land of the Dead after sneaking into a mausoleum and strumming his musical idol's old guitar. He ends up crossing paths with the spirit of his great-great-grandfather, attempting to get his help in order to return to the world of the living, while also trying to reverse a familial ban on music instilled when he was young.

Now, nine years after the movie was first released in theaters, Coco has returned to the public consciousness thanks to its latest milestone on streaming. According to data from November 12, 2026, Coco has crossed 50 days on Disney+ in the United States. The Pixar movie currently sits at Number 9 on the platform in the US, while also retaining a Number 5 spot worldwide. It's clear that, even long after the movie was originally released, the film still resonates with a wide audience around the world.

It's not too surprising, either, considering reviews for Coco have been overwhelmingly positive from both critics and audiences alike. Its critical acclaim stems from the movie's beautiful animation, strong voice acting, catchy music, and an emotional story about family that resonates with audiences of all ages. The film also has a clear, deep respect for Mexican culture that comes out in its story. These elements have aided in its success, and have justified why it's becoming Pixar's next franchise.

In March 2025, Disney's then-CEO Bob Iger confirmed that Coco 2 was in development. It was later confirmed the movie will be released on November 21, 2029, 12 years after the first movie came out. While no plot details have been confirmed as of writing, it has been reported that Benjamin Bratt will be reprising his role as Ernesto, Miguel's idol whom he meets in the Land of the Dead. Even without any aspect of the story getting confirmed, the movie already sounds like a promising follow-up.

Since Coco is still doing well on streaming almost a decade after its theatrical release, it seems like the movie has what it takes to remain popular until the sequel arrives. The film has retained a major streak in the US and a massive presence around the world, confirming there's always going to be an audience for it. And, when it comes to the Pixar film's quality, that audience is tapped in on what makes the movie such an important part of its history.

#3432. Florida Convicted Sex Offender Up For Execution 28 Years After Killing 7-Year-Old Girl

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis signed off on a death warrant for Willie Seth Crain Jr., a man convicted of kidnapping and murdering a 7-year-old girl in 1998 ... whose body has never been found.

Crain is now scheduled to be executed on December 10, 2026 … more than 28 years after the little girl’s disappearance.

Per court docs, Crain met Kathryn Hartman at a Hillsborough County bar in September 1998.

Just two days later, on September 10, Hartman invited Crain over for dinner, where she introduced him to her 7-year-old daughter, Amanda Brown.

The three later went to Crain’s trailer before returning to Hartman’s home, where she invited him to spend the night because he’d been drinking.

According to the court documents, all three slept in the same bed ... but when Hartman woke up around 6:15 the following morning because of an alarm, both Crain and Amanda were missing.

Hartman called Crain at his home around 6:30 a.m., but he claimed he had no idea where Amanda was. He told her he was “leaving to hook up his boat” and would call her later.

According to the documents, Crain claimed he left Hartman’s home around 1:30 a.m. and returned to his trailer, where he began cleaning – something he insisted was normal for him to do at that time. He also claimed he accidentally “spilled some bleach” while cleaning.

Crain told investigators he left his home around 4:45 a.m. and arrived at the Courtney Campbell Causeway in Tampa Bay around 5:15 a.m. ... despite Hartman saying he answered the phone at his home around 6:30 a.m.

Detectives later located Crain out on Tampa Bay and brought him back to shore for questioning.

Investigators noticed fresh scratches on both of his elbows and another on his left arm. When questioned about the injuries and Amanda’s disappearance, Crain claimed he didn’t know how he got hurt or what had happened to the girl.

According to Tampa Bay's News 10, investigators believe Crain dumped Amanda’s body into Old Tampa Bay, where he worked as a commercial fisherman setting crab traps.Prosecutors said traces of Amanda’s blood were discovered inside Crain’s bathroom and on his boxer shorts.

Within weeks of Amanda’s disappearance, Crain was arrested and charged with kidnapping and first-degree murder.

And this wasn’t Crain’s first run-in with the law involving children.

According to court records, Crain had previously been convicted of sexual offenses involving underage girls in 1984.

Despite extensive efforts to locate Amanda, her body was never found.

On September 13, 1999, a jury found Crain guilty of first-degree murder and kidnapping. Two months later, he was sentenced to death for Amanda’s murder and received a life sentence for her kidnapping.

Crain later appealed his conviction, arguing prosecutors had failed to present sufficient evidence of premeditation. However, in 2005, the Florida Supreme Court upheld his convictions and sentences.

Now, more than 28 years after Amanda vanished, Crain is scheduled to be executed on December 10, 2026, at 6 p.m. If it happens, it will mark Florida’s 22nd execution this year, setting a new record for the state.

#3430. Apple staff accused of signing up customers to subscriptions without consent; company responds

Repair technician turned consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann recently accused Apple store staff of signing up customers to the company’s services subscriptions without their consent.

Apple has not yet commented, but has taken two steps indicating that the company takes the accusations seriously …

Rossmann is a repair technician who specializes in component-level logic board repairs and data recovery. He later became a key figure in advocating for right-to-repair legislation, which Apple initially opposed and later backed.

In a recent video, he claimed that some Apple store staff were signing up customers to trials of paid services subscriptions without their informed consent. Targets set by Apple are said to have encouraged the practice.

Customers accepting the offer of a personalized shopping experience could be shown the free trials of Apple services available to them based on their recent purchases. For example, buying an iPhone currently entitles you to a free three-month subscription to Apple TV. However, these trials automatically start debiting your payment method if you don’t cancel them before they end.

Staff were instructed to show these offers to customers and were allegedly set a 40% sign-up target, which Apple tracked as a performance metric. Crucially, the offers are shown on the employee’s device rather than on the customer’s phone. A store member told Rossman that some staff were hitting the Accept button without properly obtaining consent from customers in order to hit their target.

When I asked whether they’d seen a specialist press Agree with their own eyes, they answered “Yes, I saw some specialists press on behalf of the customer. So, they are hitting agree. They are signing the customer up to something without actually having the customer click okay, hit okay, or provide express consent.”

The store member also claimed that staff were describing the offer as a gift, which further disguised the fact that it would turn into a paid recurring subscription unless canceled.

This is not shocking to me. Apple started pushing subscriptions during the sales process years ago when I worked in the stores.

I remember this being a major shift from being more customer focused over to becoming a battleground of a sales floor trying to get your "numbers". I even recall hearing that someone got promoted because their numbers were "so good" while we all knew they were signing people for AC+ without their knowledge. Sad days.

At the time of writing, Apple has not responded directly to the accusations, but in a follow-up video yesterday Rossman cites a staff member describing the company’s response.

He says a memo was read out in the morning meeting stating that only customers could press the Accept button, and internal systems indicate Apple is no longer grading staff on the signup metric.

We have reached out to Apple for comment and will update with any response.

Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.

#3427. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3426. Apple pushing faster on agentic Siri would carry three big risks

Yesterday saw two reports about Apple software development. The first said that the company was aiming to give Siri more agentic capabilities “as soon as next year,” while the second said that CEO John Ternus is pushing Craig Federighi to speed up software development.

If accurate, it seems near-certain the two reports are connected. But if Ternus really is pushing for an acceleration in Siri’s ability to act as an AI agent, that comes with three potentially huge risks …

Both reports were by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, though he didn’t directly connect them. On the Siri side, his newsletter contrasted the agentic abilities of some competitor models, suggesting that Apple ultimately wants to achieve the same things.

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year.

The report about Ternus pushing Federighi for faster software development mentions “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” of which agentic capabilities would be the obvious candidate.

But agentic capabilities are among the most dangerous forms of AI given the multitude of things that could go very, very wrong.

The most obvious is simply failing to carry out the task. Depending on the importance of it, the consequences could range from annoyance through to significant harm.

Technology has long failed to live up to one of its biggest promises: relieving us of mundane work in order to devote our time to more fulfilling things. For example, obtaining tickets to a popular gig or other event, which currently involves scheduling time in order to repeatedly refresh a page, perhaps wait through a queuing system, and finally carry out the transaction. It would be great to be able to hand this off to an AI.

But even on something relatively unimportant like this, if we delegated the task and the AI failed to obtain the tickets, especially if this was due to a silly error, this could prove enormously frustrating. If the task were more important, the results could obviously be far worse.

Potentially even worse is achieving the task but doing so in inappropriate ways. We’ve already seen high-profile examples of this, like the Hugging Face hack caused by an AI model seeking so hard to carry out instructions that it used underhand methods to bypass crucial safeguards in the process.

Over two thousand real secrets, including passwords, API tokens, SSH root logins, and even admin-level cloud keys, were found leaking on GitHub after developers clicked “Yes, and don’t ask again” in Claude Code […] When a developer grants Claude Code permission to proceed with “Yes, and don’t ask again,” it saves the exact command, including secrets, to a file, .claude/settings.local.json, inside the project folder. This file should never be exposed publicly [but] Apiiro, an application security company, found 104,185 public copies of such files on GitHub across 103,617 repositories.

This was just a few days after Anthropic started encouraging Claude users to connect their bank and finance card accounts to the AI chatbot. (My own answer is “Hell, no.”)

When we delegate a task to an AI system that requires access to any of our personal data, and we’re not expected to check on it again until the task is complete, the potential for disaster here is enormous.

It’s worth prefixing this with a note that the reliability of the paired reports is far from certain. In particular, in a closed-door meeting between Ternus and Federighi, it’s hard to see how the content could have leaked unless one of the two men chose to do this. If Ternus leaked it, that suggests a very high level of frustration on his part. But leaving that aside …

I hope Ternus is pushing Federighi for improved software quality and not just new features...

We’re currently witnessing an AI arms race, with each company aiming to beat its competitors to next-generation capabilities, even while acknowledging a non-trivial possibility that the pace of development could put humanity’s future at risk.

In my view, the very last thing we need is Apple joining this race. I know it can be frustrating when Apple lags behind other companies in the introduction of some types of new tech, but this is one field in which I would be very happy to see Apple proceed very much more cautiously than others.

What’s your view on this? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3425. The Mandalorian’s New Release Returns To An Abandoned George Lucas Star Wars TV Show

Six months after The Mandalorian and Grogu brought Pedro Pascal's Din Djarin and his ward Grogu to the big screen, they're back in a new Star Wars release. Since 2019, after the end of the sequel trilogy, we've been in The Mandalorian era of Star Wars. The Lucasfilm TV show was essentially Disney+'s flagship series, and it's so very appropriate that the beloved pair brought the franchise back to the big screen ahead of next year's Starfighter. The Mandalorian and Grogu's box office may have been disappointing, but the film has found new success on Disney+.

Lucasfilm has now published The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu, a celebration of the series that showcases its development. These art books are always must-buys, and this is no exception; it features stunning double-page spreads of everything from the Hutt homeworld of Nal Hutta to alternate designs for characters and aliens. Most delightfully, The Art of The Mandalorian and Grogu also reveals a George Lucas subplot that was sadly abandoned (but seems to have been incorporated into a tie-in Smugglers' Run mission at Galaxy's Edge).

It seems scripts for The Mandalorian and Grogu initially took the pair to the galactic capital of Coruscant itself, where they'd have confronted Imperial agents on Level 1313. This would have been a very different Coruscant to the city-planet seen in the prequels; the lower levels of Coruscant are a hive of scum and villainy, and it makes sense that the Empire would be active there. Indeed, I'd even suggest this was explicitly set up in The Mandalorian season 3, in a subplot involving Imperial spy Elia Kane.

In the end, this idea was dropped. Jon Favreau felt the New Republic military would handle Imperial unrest on Coruscant themselves, rather than sending a bounty hunter. While I understand his argument, I'm not entirely convinced, given the New Republic did ultimately lose Coruscant to Imperial sympathizers (it's why the city-planet was no longer galactic capital by The Force Awakens). Amusingly, there is still a Coruscant mission in The Mandalorian and Grogu's Smuggler's Run tie-in, so the idea wasn't fully abandoned.

Level 1313 is a matter of Star Wars legend. Back in the early 2000s, George Lucas planned to release the first-ever live-action Star Wars TV show, Underworld, which would have been set on level 1313. This would have explored the galaxy's seedier underbelly, albeit set during the Dark Times of the Empire's reign. Dave Filoni recreated level 1313 in animated form in The Clone Wars season 7, and it seems we almost got this abandoned Lucas concept in The Mandalorian and Grogu as well.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but prices aren’t always what they seem. Use a price tracker to make sure you’re getting the best deal, or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

As 2026 winds down, the big-budget fantasy adaptations have only continued rolling in. Last month saw the release of LAIKA's long-gestating stop-motion rendition of Wildwood to overwhelming acclaim from both critics and audiences, while November has marked the arrival of the Indian epic Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, the first part of a duology that clocks in as the country's most expensive undertaking ever.
