Even as the calendar flips over, the streak will stay alive with a much-anticipated, if controversial, epic starring The Acolyte lead, Amandla Stenberg.

On January 15, Children of Blood and Bone will finally get its time in the sun with Gina Prince-Bythewood's fantasy epic adaptation in theaters. Paramount has been slowly building up buzz for the star-studded film, based on one of the most popular and acclaimed YA novels of the past ten years from bestselling author Tomi Adeyemi. Last month, the cast, led by Thuso Mbedu, Damson Idris, Tosin Cole, and Stenberg, appeared at New York Comic Con to tease the painstaking work to bring the world of Orïsha to life, from the elaborate costumes to the dazzling effects and extensive fight training. Now, Zélie Adebola's (Mbedu) story is getting another look with two months remaining until release.

Paramount has shared a new trailer showcasing Children of Blood and Bone's magic, African mythology-inspired world in stunning fashion. At the center is Zélie, a young woman who witnessed the magic of her kingdom be violently ripped away by its ruthless king, Saran (Chiwetel Ejiofor), leaving her without a mother. Saran created a society where the magically-inclined divîners have no power, and the few allowed to survive are forced into lives of poverty and oppression. To restore what her people lost and save Orïsha, she and her brother join forces with the King's own son and daughter to oppose his reign of terror.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Alongside the main stars standing against King Saran, the fantasy epic also features Cynthia Erivo, Lashana Lynch, Zackary Momoh, Richard Mofe-Damijo, Regina King, Idris Elba, Viola Davis, and many more among its massive ensemble. All three of Mbedu, Davis, and Lynch also worked with Prince-Bythewood on her last film, The Woman King, in 2022. All the award-worthy firepower on Children of Blood and Bone is finally poised to get the ambitious fantasy adaptation across the finish line after years of the project languishing in development hell and changing hands from the Disney umbrella to Paramount. Despite co-writing the script, however, Adeyemi ultimately distanced herself from the production this summer, saying she would not continue "being hurt and attacked behind the scenes" and citing a rift with Stenberg specifically.

Children of Blood and Bone takes over theaters on January 15. Check out the new trailer in the player above.

#3422. Jason Sudeikis and Olivia Wilde's Former Nanny Gets Nothing in Battle

Jason Sudeikis and Olivia Wilde's former nanny lost all of her claims against the actors in a lengthy arbitration battle … TMZ has learned.

According to court documents obtained by TMZ ... Jason and Olivia have filed a petition asking a New York judge to formally confirm portions of an arbitration ruling that went overwhelmingly in their favor against former nanny Ericka Genaro.

Here's the deal ... Ericka sued Jason and Olivia in California in February 2023, claiming she was wrongfully terminated after the couple's breakup allegedly increased her childcare responsibilities and caused her significant stress and anxiety. She claimed Sudeikis fired her after she requested a three-day medical leave.

Jason and Olivia fought back, arguing that Genaro had signed a confidentiality agreement requiring employment disputes to be handled privately through binding arbitration in New York rather than in a California courtroom.

Eventually they got what they wanted ... a California judge ordered the dispute into private arbitration in New York, where the couple would ultimately prevail.

The couple just filed a petition asking a New York judge to confirm the arbitration ruling, which denied all of Ericka's requests for damages and dismissed all eight of her claims. The arbitrator also found she willfully breached her confidentiality agreement and awarded Jason and Olivia more than $1.27 million in damages, legal fees and costs.  The former couple is not seeking to enforce the monetary award in this latest filing because of Genaro's bankruptcy.

The arbitration is over, and Jason and Olivia are now asking a New York judge to make the key rulings official, potentially bringing this lengthy legal battle closer to an end.

#3420. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3416. Apple now sells ‘innovative’ game controller play pad and 20+ more accessories

Apple has updated its third-party accessories lineup ahead of the holidays. The refreshed lineup includes products for gaming, iPhone filmmaking, charging, and more. Among the most interesting additions is an “innovative” game controller that works with iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, Apple Vision Pro, and more.

The GAMR Active Game Controller retails for $199.95 at Apple. Apple describes it as an “innovative, pressure-sensitive game controller play pad” that lets players control compatible games by stepping and moving across nine responsive zones.

Those zones map to directional controls and the A, B, X, and Y buttons of a traditional controller. GAMR connects over Bluetooth to iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, Mac, and Apple Vision Pro, with support for compatible Apple Arcade and App Store games. There’s also a free GAMR app with original games.

Apple lists up to eight to ten hours of battery life, and the pad rolls up for storage between gaming sessions. Think a dance mat-style approach to playing games across Apple’s devices.

Another notable addition is the ShiftCam ProRig Filmmaker Kit, which sells for $169.95 in Titanium Silver.

The kit puts an open frame around your iPhone, with repositionable handles for shooting in landscape or portrait. A Bluetooth shutter lets you capture shots from the grip, while two cold shoe mounts and six quarter-inch mounting points provide room for lights, microphones, tripods, and other accessories.

ShiftCam also includes an adapter for compatible filters and lenses, a carrying pouch, and interchangeable bumpers for iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

For something smaller and more affordable, Apple now sells the ShiftCam SnapPocket Light 2 Magnetic LED Ring Light for $39.95.

The pocket-sized light attaches to a MagSafe-compatible iPhone or case and flips 180 degrees to illuminate either you or your subject. It offers five brightness levels and five color temperature settings ranging from warm to cool, with a built-in battery that recharges over USB-C. ShiftCam also includes a magnetic ring sticker for attaching it to an iPad or MacBook.

The light is also included in the $159.95 ShiftCam SnapTravel Kit Pro 2, alongside a camera grip with a 5,000mAh battery and Qi2 charging, a selfie stick that converts into a tripod, and a travel pouch.

Elsewhere, Apple’s latest accessory selection includes two Belkin power banks. The $99.95 UltraCharge Pro 20K features an integrated USB-C cable with up to 70W output and two additional USB-C ports. The $49.95 BoostCharge Slim Magnetic Power Bank 5K with Stand offers 15W Qi2 wireless charging, 20W wired charging, and a built-in kickstand.

There’s also the $49.95 MOFT Snap Field MagSafe Wallet Stand, which holds up to eight cards and unfolds into a stand for your iPhone. You can also find it on Amazon.

Cases and bags round out the selection, including Tech21 FlexFolio and mophie Knit folios for iPad Air and iPad Pro, a Tech21 EvoShell for MacBook Neo, Rains sleeves, and Herschel sleeves, bags, and organizers.

#3414. Taylor Sheridan’s ‘Yellowstone’ Spin-Off Officially Returns After Surprise Break

When it was reported that Yellowstone was ending, no one knew what the future would look like for what was once the biggest show on television. There were internal wrangles, and after five years, it seemed like some cast and crew members were ready for something different. So it came as a bit of a surprise when CBS and Paramount announced a new spin-off, but it wouldn't be like anything viewers had seen before. The new series would take a procedural approach and would follow one of the least explored characters in the flagship series, Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes).

The problem was that Grimes wasn't interested in playing Kayce after Yellowstone, and he had been vocal about it. "I didn’t think I wanted to come back to it, because I felt like Kayce’s story ended so perfectly in the first show," the actor admitted in an interview with THR. "And I was like, well, what are we gonna do now? He’s got his dream life. Everything he’s been fighting for, he’s gotten. He literally rode off into the sunset. And what sort of breaks that world open for him is that that dream life became no longer possible." With a bit of convincing from showrunner Spencer Hudnut and support from Taylor Sheridan, Grimes put the cowboy hat back on, and Marshals arrived earlier this year, becoming a ratings juggernaut for CBS.

Season 2 airs this fall, but the network announced the show would take a two-week break, meaning no new episode on Sunday, November 8. However, Marshals is back on schedule this Sunday, November 15, with an episode that could become a turning point for some character dynamics. In Marshals Season 2, Episode 5, "Roughstock," Cal (Logan Marshall-Green) goes to Salt Lake to see a cancer specialist, and Belle (Arielle Kebbel) tags along without anyone else knowing. Is this the beginning of a new romance, and what effect will it have on the team? Meanwhile, Andrea (Ash Santos) temporarily takes the reins in Cal's absence, and problems arise when Kayce steps outside the marshal's jurisdiction to help his friend Mo (Mo Brings Plenty) after Mo's nephew goes missing.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

After this break, the show will air uninterrupted until around the holiday period. On November 22, the team is back together, and this time Kayce and Belle go undercover. There will be some guest appearances from Beau Knapp, Judd Lormand, Marque Richardson, and Carter Faith. On November 29, the team hunts down an international fugitive. Meanwhile, Kayce starts a new project while his relationship with Tate (Brecken Merrill) remains strained. Scarlett Burke guest stars.

Watch new episodes of Marshals on Sundays on CBS and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3408. Late Billionaire Ted Turner: Ex-Wife Jane Fonda Not Named in 2025 Will

Late businessman Ted Turner was married and divorced three times during his life ... but the final version of his will made no mention of his last and legendary ex-wife, Jane Fonda ... TMZ has learned.

Ted’s children, Laura, Robert, Rhett, Reed and Sara, filed a petition to be named executors of the CNN founder’s estate. They were the only listed heirs to Ted’s fortune.

The filing notes that Ted was married three times during his life. His ex-wives included Judy Nye, who he divorced in 1964, Jane Turner, who he split with in 1988, and Jane Fonda, but the marriage ended in 2001.

Jane is not listed as a beneficiary to the estate ... despite her raving about her ex-husband for years after the split ... and praising him after he passed.

Ted reportedly made several changes to his trust, which was first drafted in 2003, when he was 64. He changed the trust again in 2005 … made more changes in 2006 and 2007 … and again in 2009, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and his final amendment in 2025.

Ted instructed his heirs to pay his debts and handle business matters ... but noted, “I have confidence in the investments which will be found in my estate at the time of my death,” but said they could sell off assets, if needed.

#3407. 5 Years Later, the Final ‘Outlander’ Book Officially Still Has No Release Date

Of all the epic conclusions in 2026, from Prime Video's The Boys to HBO's Emmy-favorite Hacks, perhaps the most satisfying was one final outing in Starz's hit series, Outlander. Based on Diana Gabaldon's book series of the same name, this blend of time travel, sci-fi, fantasy, and romance had viewers hooked for 12 years, growing from strength to strength each season as more became invested in the lives of Caitríona Balfe's (Belfast, Ford v Ferrari) Claire and Sam Heughan's (The Spy Who Dumped Me, Love Again) Jamie.

"The final season resembles more of a warm, reassuring hug for viewers," wrote Collider's Carly Lane in her review, one of many gushing with praise for Outlander's last mainline move. The final outing also opened to nearly 3 million multi-platform viewers, making it the number one scripted cable program of the week, and proving that the love for this franchise has not yet diminished, even if the eighth season had to end with an original, full-circle conclusion penned by the show writers, as Gabaldon hadn't yet completed the long-awaited Book 10.

Six months on from the Outlander Season 8 finale, has the mind behind this enthralling fantasy tale managed to complete her final installment? Sadly, the answer is no, with there still being no confirmed release date for A Blessing for a Warrior Going Out. Gabaldon has previously admitted that an 800-page conclusion requires plenty of time and attention, not least for extensive background and historical research purposes. There is hope that a release date might arrive in 2027, but nothing is confirmed, and with a nearly-5-year gap between the last book and today, it's important not to get our hopes up just yet.

Outlander star Balfe turned her attention to another novel adaptation earlier this Fall season, as she starred alongside Normal People's Daisy Edgar-Jones and Pond Life's Esmé Creed-Miles in the latest big-screen take on Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility. #3406. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3395. 8 People Dead, 17 Others Injured in NYC Building Collapse, Pregnant Woman Survives

The massive building collapse Wednesday in NYC claimed the lives of at least eight people and left at least 17 others injured, including 3 firefighters and 7 kids, officials said, but a pregnant woman survived.

The New York Fire Department said the apartment building -- established in the 1930s in Flatbush, Brooklyn -- crumbled to the ground Wednesday afternoon. The cause of the collapse is still under investigation.

According to the FDNY, firefighters raced to the scene, searching for survivors in the rubble. Firefighters pulled people to safety along with a 6-month pregnant woman. Her husband was seen crying tears of joy while embracing another person upon learning that his wife was alive.

During their search efforts, firefighters discovered several people dead and 17 injured, with some in critical condition, the FDNY said. The agency noted that 7 of the victims were children, with several other people unaccounted for.

FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said the number of victims could change “by the minute” as the operation -- expected to take days -- moves forward. Bonsignore also vowed to "look until we find everybody,” adding that construction workers -- who were inside the building at the time -- were among the victims.

#3393. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3389. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3387. MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe wallet is built for the people who still carry cash

I’ve been on a Pelican kick this fall. It started with the Pelican MagSafe Wallet, then the Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack, and the reason is pretty simple: once the weather turns cool, I want iPhone accessories built for the outdoors because I am outside more. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is really helpful is you want something rugged, but also supports holding cash.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most magnetic wallets are a simple card sleeve and nothing else. If you carry a few $5 bills for tips, cash-only places, etc., you end up folding them around a card and hoping they don’t slip out. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet has a stainless steel money clip on the outside of the wallet, so the cash rides on the back, where you can access it without pulling your credit cards out. It’s the same hard-shell construction as the rest of Pelican’s lineup, with the same MagSafe magnets.

The wallet holds up to five cards, which is just about perfect for my use cases. That covers my Driver’s license, debit card, and a few credit cards. There are ridges inside that push the cards up when you squeeze, so you’re not digging with your nails. A steel plate blocks RFID scanning, and the shell is rated IPX4 for water, which covers rain, etc.

Pelican calls its drop protection military-grade, which is what every accessory company says. A more useful way to think about it is that it’s a hard-shell wallet rather than a leather or silicone one.

Two things to know going in with this wallet. Five cards plus a clip of cash makes for a thick back on your phone, so this isn’t a very slim wallet. If you’re replacing a money clip, you are basically combining the two into one.

If you never carry much cash, the original Pelican wallet is the better pick. If you do want to carry a bunch of cash, the Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is an awesome pickup.

#3381. Apple to open new Developer Center in Istanbul as part of broader Turkey investment

Apple today announced a long-term investment in Turkey, with seven new facilities focused on app development and manufacturing set to open in the country starting next year. Here are the details.

In a press release issued on its Turkish Newsroom (via MacRumors), Apple today announced a series of long-term investments in Turkey.

The announcement comes as former CEO and current executive chairman Tim Cook visits the country, as he’s been sharing on X.

Merhaba Istanbul! What a stunning view from the Grand Bazaar this morning alongside talented creator Cem Başak. Thrilled to visit this remarkable country! pic.twitter.com/c4daBBXe1l

The company’s investment in Turkey will be three-pronged, with the opening of five new Apple Developer Academies, one Apple Developer Center, and one Apple Manufacturing Academy.

Apple says it will open five new developer academies across Turkey over the next three years, with the first opening in Istanbul in 2027, alongside its new developer center. The Apple Manufacturing Academy, meanwhile, is set to open in Ankara in 2028.

Here’s Cook commenting on today’s announcement (translation ours):

“Apple has been serving our customers and communities in Turkey for 35 years. With this new commitment, we are proud to support the next generation of innovative entrepreneurs in the years ahead. […] Turkey’s developer community is developing apps used around the world. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized businesses stand out as organizations creating opportunities throughout the country. This investment provides developers and businesses with access to the training and resources they need to take their brightest ideas even further, as well as to Apple experts.”

Apple explained that its developer academies will offer “free, intensive nine-month programs focused on coding, design, marketing, project management, and artificial intelligence technologies,” while the developer center “will provide developers, entrepreneurs, and start-ups with a hands-on learning experience by providing access to the latest tools, technologies, and resources, as well as Apple experts and events.”

As for its manufacturing academy in Ankara, which will mark the company’s first Apple Manufacturing Academy outside the US, it will “provide free training and consultancy to small and medium-sized businesses, students and innovative entrepreneurs.”

Led by Apple experts, the curriculum will help participants adopt AI and intelligent manufacturing techniques through courses on machine learning technology, predictive maintenance, advanced automation, and robotics, as well as interactive workshops on lean operations and production efficiency.

Pete Hegseth was in a celebratory mood after Republicans successfully blocked his impeachment in the House of Representatives on Tuesday night, gloating with Donald Trump about the failed effort to boot him from the Pentagon. The following day called for a more solemn demeanor, however, as Hegseth and Trump visited Arlington National Cemetery to commemorate Veterans Day.

Hegseth’s party didn’t get the memo. On Wednesday afternoon, CNN released footage of an Army sentinel castigating Hegseth and his advisers when they started laughing after taking photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Solider, one of the nation’s most sacred war memorials.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!” the sentinel yelled shortly after laughter emanated from Hegseth’s group, before the group continued up the steps in front of the memorial.

"All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!"A Sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier yells after laughter could be heard from a group near Secretary Hegseth, who was taking posed photographs at the site. pic.twitter.com/SYs4q6GxK9

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery is a burial site for an American soldier who died during World War I. An Army sentinel from the Third Infantry has guarded the tomb 24 hours a day since 1948, with a guard-changing taking place every half hour.

Hegseth was standing in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, his chief of staff, Ricky Buria, his deputy chief of staff, Patrick Weaver, and his senior adviser and deputy assistant, Tami Radabaugh, following a Veterans Day ceremony at the site, per CNN. #3375. Jaren Johnston Is Releasing a Solo Album. What Does That Mean for the Cadillac Three?

When the Cadillac Three walked offstage at the Born and Raised Festival in Pryor, Oklahoma, on Sept. 13, 2024, fans of the Southern rock band didn’t realize they’d just witnessed the trio’s last public performance. A week later, the Nashville band announced they were canceling the remainder of the year’s gigs so that singer-guitarist Jaren Johnston could prioritize his health. The group has yet to return to the road.

Johnston, a songwriter behind radio hits like Tim McGraw’s “Meanwhile Back at Mama’s” and Keith Urban’s “You Gonna Fly,” had been through the wringer. His father, the musician Jerry Ray Johnston, died at 65 in 2022, and the Cadillac Three’s busy touring schedule didn’t allow the frontman time to heal. The future of the group, known for hard-hitting songs like “Tennessee Mojo” and “White Lightning,” was in doubt. Drummer Neil Mason pivoted to songwriting and artist management; lap-steel player/bassist Kelby Ray played guitar in the house band for Taylor Sheridan’s country-music series The Road.

This Friday, Johnston will resurface with his debut solo album, The Guest Room, a collection of 13 songs written and recorded in the spare room of his home.

So, where does that leave the Cadillac Three? Johnston tells Rolling Stone’s Nashville Now podcast the band members are slowly starting to pick up the pieces.

“The three of us just want the best for the three of us, each one of us. When I had to come off the road, they understood,” he says. “Obviously [they were] not happy about not being able to play shows and not being able to explain to everybody why. But they probably saw it coming, a little bit.”

Johnston says he, Mason, and Ray met at a local Mexican restaurant in Nashville recently to reconnect. “All we did was sit and laugh for an hour and a half,” he says. “You can’t mess that whole thing up.”

#3372. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3371. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.

They prioritize driving performance over everything

I’ve said it countless times this year: If there’s one type of vehicle I’ve driven more than anything else, it’s the 3-row family hauler. When you’re looking for maximum passenger capacity without skimping on comfort, full-size SUVs certainly fit the bill — and the Nissan Armada and Dodge Durango are no exception.

Unlike mainstream models like the Chevrolet Tahoe or GMC Yukon Denali that prioritize plush comfort over driving dynamics — often making them feel like lumbering giants — these two are far from it. Instead, these heavyweights prove that family practicality and raw enthusiasm can genuinely coexist.

The $55,225 as-tested 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition delivers pure old-school muscle with a 475-hp 6.4-liter HEMI V8 engine that sounds genuinely imposing. That looks like a steal next to the $83,735 as-tested price of the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo, but the Nismo counters with a twin-turbo V6 pushing 460 horsepower, sharper styling, and enough high-tech amenities to make a case for its steeper sticker.

After testing each one for a week, only one earns my recommendation.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

NISMO-Tuned 3.5L Twin-Turbo V6 Engine (4WD)

17 mpg city / 16 mpg highway / 19 mpg combined

13 mpg city / 19 mpg highway / 15 mpg combined

Frankly, neither design captured my attention at first — but one of them eventually grew on me. Even though they compete in the full-size, 3-row segment, they take entirely different styling routes.

The 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition leans hard into classic muscle swagger — reminiscent of the Dodge Charger — with its scooped performance hood, functional air intakes, bold Brembo brake calipers, and a rounded profile that still looks surprisingly menacing. It catches plenty of glances thanks to that aggressive stance, but it lacks the visual flair to truly sell me on its familiar look.

Between the two, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo gets my nod. Despite its noticeably more upright, boxy proportions, it delivers far more drama and curb appeal. Nissan gave it the full NISMO treatment, outfitting the SUV with massive 22-inch machined alloy wheels, an aggressive front fascia and grille, sculpted side steps with flared fenders, and full-width LED taillights. The sharp two-tone premium paint finish seals the deal, transforming this traditionally square full-size SUV into an imposing showstopper worthy of a cameo in a Fast & Furious flick.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

Nobody shops for performance-tuned, three-row SUVs with the intent of saving on fuel. However, one of these gas-guzzlers still proved friendlier at the pump over the long haul.

The 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition surprised me most on dedicated highway runs, achieving a best mark of 24.2 mpg and handily overdelivering on its 19-mpg highway rating. On short-distance trips, I averaged 21.6 mpg — equally impressive given its 13-mpg city EPA estimate. Overall, it managed 18.1 mpg across 237.9 total miles of mixed driving.

In comparison, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo made a much stronger case for real-world consistency. While its best recorded long-distance run of 23.9 mpg fell just shy of the Dodge, its twin-turbo V6 and 9-speed automatic worked far more efficiently across everyday traffic. Over the course of 302 miles of mixed driving, the Armada Nismo delivered an average of 19.9 mpg — not only beating its official 17-mpg combined EPA rating, but also comfortably edging out the Durango by nearly two full miles per gallon overall. When you’re feeding a sport-tuned hauler week in and week out, that spread makes a noticeable difference.

When SUVs are slapped with performance badges, driving dynamics are what make them special over conventional haulers. While the Armada managed to surprise me in a big way, the Durango takes the crown here.

Nissan deserves immense credit for defying expectations given the Armada's boxy proportions, which initially made me apprehensive about driving it on crowded highways. It packs a genuinely strong 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6 pushing 460 horsepower and 516 lb-ft of torque, delivering instant thrust and effortless passing power.

It's also surprisingly easy to drive for its size, thanks to an ultra-responsive steering wheel that feels very light and loose. If that’s not enough, its adaptive electronic air suspension and great shocks make cruising over bumpy roads a breeze.

Yet for all the Armada’s composure, it can’t match the raw power and exhilarating feel of the 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition. Backed by a 475-horsepower 6.4-liter HEMI V8 under the hood, it completely transforms the driving experience.

Between the thunderous exhaust roar, immediate throttle response, and quick Brembo stopping power, the Durango delivers a far more thrilling ride every time I put the pedal to the metal. Honestly, it handles like a muscle car — giving enthusiasts the genuine excitement that almost every other three-row hauler lacks.

Both SUVs deliver great accommodations when it comes to passenger capacity, but one takes interior luxury and space to another level. What I love about both full-size haulers is how they offer second-row captain's chairs paired with a convenient center console for cupholders and armrest storage.

In the Dodge Durango R/T 392, second-row passengers have 38.6 inches of legroom to stretch out comfortably, while the third-row bench yields 33.5 inches. Even though adults can fit back there, my knees practically touch the seatbacks in front of me. Finally, there’s a cavernous 17.2 cubic feet of cargo space behind the third row that easily swallowed my electric scooter without needing to wedge it at an angle.

The one big downside for the Durango is that it lacks lane-centering assist when adaptive cruise control is engaged — meaning, it won't actively keep you centered between the lines.

The 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo simply offers more cabin volume to comfortably seat adults while pampering them with genuine luxury. Thanks to its taller cabin, legroom feels far more generous in the second row with 39.2 inches of space, while the third row provides 32.9 inches. The Armada also delivers significantly more cargo capacity behind the rear seats with 20.4 cubic feet of trunk space.

Between its plush, red-and-black trimmed NISMO suede seats, whisper-quiet cabin insulation, and ProPILOT Assist for hands-free highway cruising, the Armada makes long distance drices effortless no matter where you sit. That said, its lane centering isn't always spot-on when activated, but the overall luxury leap is impossible to ignore.

On paper, the pricing advantage leans heavily toward the Durango, but it's important to look at what each model actually delivers before jumping to conclusions.

Dodge’s value proposition is centered squarely on performance, yet this bargain full-size SUV still includes a respectable set of amenities. For example, you get a single-pane sunroof, a Harman Kardon sound system, and a standard backup camera. Still, I’m not as impressed with the dashboard layout, which leans far too conventional and dated.

By contrast, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo commands a steep $83,735 as-tested price that’s nearly $28,500 higher than its rival. That’s a significant stretch, but it buys a modern suite of luxury and tech features: an expansive panoramic moonroof, a high-fidelity 12-speaker Klipsch premium audio system, heated front seats, and a sophisticated 3D Enhanced Intelligent Around View Monitor that makes navigating tight parking spaces a breeze.

While the Armada undoubtedly delivers the more modern, tech-rich experience, the Durango's $55,225 as-tested price makes it an untouchable performance bargain in the three-row space.

I can’t overstate the price disparity between these two sport-tuned SUVs, with one costing nearly $28,500 more than the other. At their core, however, both deliver large family-hauling utility without forcing you to completely give up your passion for driving.

Without question, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo is the superior all-around modern SUV for everyday living. Between its sharp two-tone finish, plush suede seats, massive passenger volume, whisper-quiet cabin, and cutting-edge tech suite, it feels every bit like an $84,000 flagship that justifies its price tag. If your budget allows, the Armada won't disappoint with its effortless acceleration and smooth, composed ride — making it tough to beat.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

Yet when it comes to the vehicle I’d actually spend my own money on, the 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition gets my vote, despite coming up short on paper once all the category scores are tallied. Sure, the Durango's interior aesthetics lack the modern flair of its rival, but it unapologetically prioritizes genuine muscle car performance with three rows of seats.

With an as-tested price of $55,225, it isn’t just competitive — it's an untouchable performance bargain in a segment otherwise dominated by $60K+ land yachts.

#3369. Summer Walker’s Label LVRN Fires Back With Breach of Contract Counterclaim

The independent label that signed Grammy-nominated R&B star Summer Walker early in her career is denying allegations that it locked her into an oppressive contract and misappropriated money, and it’s firing back with its own breach of contract claim against the singer.

In a new court filing obtained and first reported by Rolling Stone, Atlanta-based Love Renaissance Records, known as LVRN, strongly denies allegations of breach of contract and fraud made by Walker in her August lawsuit. “At no time has LVRN acted in bad faith, been stubbornly litigious, or caused Walker unnecessary trouble and expense,” the new 14-page filing submitted in Fulton County, Georgia, states.

The label and management firm then accuses Walker of being the one withholding funds. According to the filing, Walker failed to pay LVRN a 15 percent share of income from business opportunities it allegedly secured for her, as well as a 20 percent share of her songwriting performance royalties. The company also claims Walker stopped paying its agreed-upon 7 percent share of proceeds from her Finally Over It tour in 2026, after she initially made such payments.

“Walker has acted in bad faith and been stubbornly litigious, such that LVRN is entitled to recover its resulting attorneys’ fees,” the new filing states. It’s asking the court to dismiss Walker’s original complaint, rule in its favor on the breach of contract counterclaim, and award damages in an amount to be determined at trial.

In a statement to Rolling Stone, Walker’s lawyer, Keith Moten, said LVRN’s counterclaim “does nothing to change the fundamental issues at the heart of Summer’s lawsuit, nor does it diminish their obligation to account for their actions.”

“It is particularly disappointing that, rather than meaningfully addressing Summer’s serious allegations, LVRN is now seeking additional money from the very artist whose talent, hard work, and success helped build its business,” he said. “We strongly dispute LVRN’s counterclaims and remain confident in the legal and factual grounds supporting Summer’s lawsuit.  She remains steadfast in her pursuit of accountability, fairness, and the freedom to move forward with her career on her terms.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Walker’s manager, Aubrey Banks, tells Rolling Stone that the musician respects the legal process but will “continue to advocate” for herself and other artists while the case is pending. “Summer is a human being before she is an artist. Like anyone else who’s devoted over a decade to their work, she deserves fair treatment, transparency, and good-faith dealings. No one wants to work for 10 years with no career advancement, raise or promotion,” Banks says. “It’s just not fair. The music industry should not be exempt from the fundamental standards of fairness, dignity, and respect we expect in every other profession.”

In her lawsuit, Walker accused LVRN of improperly diverting money from her touring, recording, marketing, and merchandising budgets, and failing to pay her revenue generated by Amazon and YouTube webpages featuring her name and likeness. She claimed the company concealed financial information, betraying the trust she placed in the label as a 19-year-old artist.

“Summer is in a new phase of her life,” Moten said in a previous statement to Rolling Stone. “She’s been through a lot in her life, personally and professionally. She’s a mother now, and she doesn’t trust blindly anymore. She’s ready to fight for herself, her freedom, and her peace.”

Walker’s lawsuit alleges breach of fiduciary duty, breach of contract, and fraudulent concealment. She is asking the court to declare her 2017 agreement with LVRN “void and unenforceable.” She’s also seeking compensatory and punitive damages in amounts to be determined by the court. Moten said he believes Walker has “very strong legal grounds for the court to order Summer’s release from her deal with LVRN.” Related Content Hegseth and Advisers Yelled at for Disrespecting Tomb of Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day ‘Dare Him to Veto It’: Democrats Are Ready to Push for Real Reform Trump Gloats as Republicans Kill Bid to Impeach Pete Hegseth After Online Uproar, Sammy Kershaw Is Invited to Walk CMA Awards Red Carpet

In a related filing last month, Interscope sued Walker in Los Angeles County Superior Court, saying her ongoing effort to exit her recording contract under California’s so-called “seven-year rule” would entitle UMG to recover damages upwards of $50 million. Walker has disputed the claims.

Walker signed with Love Renaissance on Sept. 15, 2017, and with Interscope under an expanded joint venture on Nov. 1, 2017. She went on to become a huge star, with industry experts previously telling Rolling Stone her contract terms appeared “brutal” in retrospect.

In August, Walker informed Interscope that she would soon stop working under the agreement. “This letter shall serve as official notice that, effective Aug. 27, 2026, Ms. Walker will no longer render service under the agreement by reason of the fact that the agreement is no longer enforceable,” her letter to the label said, according to court filings.

In its Oct. 9 complaint, Interscope claimed Walker’s “failure to deliver” all the recordings required under her contract would leave her liable for damages. The label, owned by UMG, said her original 2017 agreement and subsequent amendments obligated her to deliver five studio albums, with her earlier projects, Last Day of Summer and CLEAR, classified as “pre-album projects” that did not count toward that album total.

Moten previously told Rolling Stone that he and Walker were “disappointed that Interscope has chosen to pursue litigation.” He said they remained confident in her legal position and her right to challenge the continued enforceability of her recording contract with Interscope. “We intend to vigorously defend against Interscope’s claims and pursue appropriate legal relief,” he said.

Moten added that Walker plans to countersue the record label. “Summer remains open to a constructive resolution. She hopes that the matter can be resolved in a manner that respects the interests of all involved, and avoids unnecessary or prolonged litigation,” said Moten. “In the meantime, Summer remains focused on her music, her artistry, her children, and her fans.” Trending Stories Sade Are Not Attending Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Bob Dylan’s Meeting With Pope Leo: People Fixated on the Hood, But the Hands Spoke Volumes Megan Thee Stallion and Daniel Radcliffe Reunite for Season Two of ‘Reggie Dinkins’

UMG’s Los Angeles lawsuit is asking for damages of at least $50 million to be determined at trial. It’s also asking for prejudgment interest, legal costs, and any “further relief” the court finds appropriate. A hearing is set for April 15.

“While we remain hopeful that our ongoing discussions will lead to an amicable resolution, the statutory deadline makes it necessary to file suit in order to preserve the terms of our contract,” an Interscope spokesperson said in a prior statement sent to Rolling Stone. “We have great respect for Summer and her music and would welcome the opportunity to continue our successful partnership.”

#3364. Mississippi Is Sending a Democrat to the Senate

Of all the spectacular Democratic upsets in 2026 midterm elections — a statewide sweep in Texas, the first senator elected by the state of Kansas in almost a century, an underdog stunner in South Carolina — the most shocking victory of all came in Mississippi.

The race to represent the ruby red state of Mississippi in the U.S. Senate was called for Democrat Scott Colom on Wednesday, just over a week after the election. Colom, a district attorney, defeated Republican incumbent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Colom led Hyde-Smith by roughly 2,000 votes the day after the election, and steadily increased the margin before the Associated Press called the race Wednesday at 5:58 p.m. ET.

“I think that anybody who can look at the math should be able to know where this is going,” Colom told reporters on the morning after the election. “It’s going to: Scott Colom is the next United States senator. I’m confident in that.”

He was right, and the victory is especially sweet. In 2023, Colom, then a state prosecutor, was nominated by President Joe Biden to a lifetime appointment on the federal bench. That nomination was blocked by a single senator from his home state: Hyde-Smith.

Breaking with her Republican colleague, Sen. Roger Wicker, who backed Colom’s selection, Hyde-Smith cited Colom’s “opposition to legislation to protect female athletes” (a reference, apparently, to his decision to sign an open letter condemning the criminalization of gender-affirming care), as well as a single political donation he got four years prior from a PAC that had received funding from George Soros.

Three years ago, Colom wrote a letter asking Hyde-Smith to reconsider the decision; she refused. Had Hyde-Smith not spiked his nomination, Colom told The New York Times in May, “It is fair to say that I would not have resigned from the federal bench to run for Senate.”

Colom made Hyde-Smith’s tone-deaf response to the rising cost of living a centerpiece of his insurgent bid to replace her. One viral ad produced by the Colom campaign showcased Hyde-Smith’s comment, in answer to a question about the beef prices, that “You have so many proteins to choose from.” Rather than pick another protein, the spot urged voters to “Pick another senator instead.” It resonated, as Mississippians appear on Wednesday poised to do exactly that. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Up until the point in late October when President Donald Trump flew to Mississippi to rally his supporters behind Hyde-Smith’s reelection effort, few political observers expected the race to be close. Only three polls were done of the match-up, compared to dozens of surveys conducted in higher-profile contests in Michigan and Texas. But in the waning days of the campaign, as it became clear Colom was mounting an unexpectedly strong challenge, former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris both traveled to Misssippi to boost Democratic support for his bid.

Colom’s win marks the first time a Democrat has represented Mississippi in the Senate since the prominent segregationist John C. Stennis retired in the 1980s.

Colom’s victory is even more remarkable considering the fact that Ty Pinkins — the Democratic candidate for Senate in 2024 — chose to run as an Independent in the general election this fall, siphoning off nearly 20,000 votes.

In spite of those challenges — and an emergency infusion of more than a million dollars from the GOP’s Senate Leadership Fund — Colom was victorious.  Trending Stories Sade Are Not Attending Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Bob Dylan’s Meeting With Pope Leo: People Fixated on the Hood, But the Hands Spoke Volumes Megan Thee Stallion and Daniel Radcliffe Reunite for Season Two of ‘Reggie Dinkins’

Hyde-Smith herself may be more surprised than anyone by that fact: Speaking at an election night party on Tuesday, she was already celebrating, boasting to supporters, “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge and you blocked him from being a U.S. senator.”

Asked on the next morning to respond to Hyde-Smith’s premature declaration, Colom called on a classic Southern expression: “Bless her heart,” he said.

#3361. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

To read Apple’s full support document, follow this link.

#3358. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

Kimmel asked the movie star and politician if he is still a Republican early on in their conversation. “Yeah I’m a Republican, absolutely,” Schwarzenegger confirmed, explaining that a “traditional Republican is someone that admires the Republican party for having free the slaves.”

“This is the history,” he explained of the party. “This is what I’m about. Someone that has given those slaves American citizenship and has given them the right to vote is Republican.”

“This sounds like all of the opposite things the Republican party stands for now though, doesn’t it?” Kimmel responded.

“It doesn’t mean I have to change my philosophy,” Schwarzenegger said. “I have my philosophy. The Ronald Reagan philosophy, who created the air resources board in California so we can regulate our own air and reduce our greenhouse gases and pollution in California. That was done by Ronald Reagan, by a Republican. Nixon created the EPA. … So those are the kind of Republicans that used to go and work together with the Democrats and got things done. This is the kind of Republican that I am.”

“Unfortunately I think you’re the only one of them left,” Kimmel noted.

“No, I don’t think I’m the only one left,” Schwarzenegger acknowledged. “But this doesn’t mean that we should give up. The bottom line is we have just seen now what some people call the blue wave. I call it a tidal wave or a tsunami. It’s not really a wave anymore. But the bottom line of that is that now the Democrats go in there and they have the majority. And then the Republicans will go in there and they have the majority. And this is how it goes back and forth and back and forth.”
